pattern: global input{} rule (padding, min-height) applied to checkboxes misaligns labels
summary: A global 'input, select, textarea { padding; min-height: 2.5rem }' rule written by an earlier agent also hit checkboxes and radios, making labels tall with text bottom-aligned and the checkbox centred. A human user reported it with the diagnosis; fix restricted the rule and made checkbox labels centred flex rows, verified with a temporary measuring test.
cost_estimate: Part of 1 subagent run; small
design_lesson: One element (<input>) covering text fields and checkboxes means a type-agnostic selector silently styles controls it shouldn't.

pattern: flex: 1 shorthand sets flex-basis 0%, squeezes column at phone width
summary: While merging contact/chat/node pages, the UI subagent used `flex: 1` on the header's main column. Because the shorthand sets flex-basis to 0%, at 390px width the name column shrank to 152px instead of the sibling link wrapping. A later test-updating subagent caught it in a phone-width test and changed it to `flex: 1 1 12rem`.
cost_estimate: small; a few tool calls inside a ~9 min test-migration subagent
design_lesson: Shorthands with surprising implicit values (flex: 1 => basis 0%) are a recurring trap; clearer longhand defaults or lint warnings would help.

pattern: non-wrapping flex row squeezes content at narrow widths
summary: The DM chat header put back link, avatar, name/subtitle and three action buttons in one non-wrapping flex row. On a phone the name column shrank to about 55px. The user reported it with a screenshot. The agent grouped the actions, let the header wrap (flex: 1 1 12rem; min-width:0), added a page.viewport phone-width test asserting the name width is over 180px, checked that the test fails on the old code, and looked at a screenshot.
cost_estimate: About 4 minutes and roughly 35 tool calls including test reruns. 8.7k output tokens.
design_lesson: Layout bugs at other viewport sizes only show up if the agent renders at those sizes. Cheap, standard 'render at N widths and flag overflow or squeezed text' tooling would surface this before a human does.

api: CSS inline layout / font fallback (emoji vs text glyphs)
pattern: mixed emoji and text-symbol icons fall back to fonts with different line heights, misaligning labels
summary: The mobile bottom nav used emoji icons (💬, 👥) next to text symbols (⚙, #). On the user's phone those fell back to fonts with different line heights, so the 'Settings' label sat lower than the others. The user reported it. The agent fixed it with a fixed-height icon box and nowrap labels, and added a headless-Chromium test that fails without the fix.
cost_estimate: About 35 tool calls, about 5k output tokens, about 8 min, including one hung vitest invocation.
design_lesson: Emoji vs text presentation and per-glyph font fallback metrics are invisible in code; a way to normalize glyph box metrics, or lint/devtools warnings for mixed-font icon rows, would prevent this.

pattern: absolutely-positioned tooltip overflows container / overlaps controls at narrow width
summary: Agent built an HTML bar-chart tooltip positioned with left:% + translateX(-50%) above the bar. A first edge-clamp heuristic (translateX -10%/-90%) still overflowed; only after rendering throwaway screenshot tests in light/dark/narrow did it see the tooltip covering the range toggle, then moved it inside the plot and clamped after measurement. It also found the selected toggle used a text-on-solid-accent token on a soft tint, making it nearly invisible.
cost_estimate: ~3 edit/screenshot iterations, ~10 tool calls, ~4 min (16:59-17:03)
design_lesson: Layout primitives for 'keep this popup inside its container' (e.g. CSS anchor positioning with fallbacks) remove the need for screenshot-driven trial and error.

pattern: build tool lowers light-dark() to media queries, so a data-theme override no longer applies to the page background
summary: Phase 12 agent noted that lightningcss compiles light-dark() in index.html into prefers-color-scheme media-query variables, so the page background outside <mc-app> follows the OS theme rather than the user's explicit data-theme setting. Left unfixed as pre-existing.
cost_estimate: Noted only
design_lesson: Features whose semantics depend on runtime state (color-scheme) shouldn't be silently down-levelled; feature detection/baseline status needs to flow into build tooling.

pattern: native platform feature distrusted (cross-browser support and timing); reimplemented by hand and native one disabled
summary: When rows are prepended to the live packet log, the user asked that the visible rows not jump, and to research the most reliable approach. After 2 web searches the agent concluded that native scroll anchoring only reached Safari in v27 and 'can fight manual scrollTop changes'. It turned native anchoring off with overflow-anchor:none and hand-rolled anchoring: record the first visible row's getBoundingClientRect in Lit willUpdate, then window.scrollBy the delta in updated(). A MutationObserver test checks this happens in the same microtask.
cost_estimate: 2 web searches, about 4 minutes, roughly 25 tool calls. 16k output tokens. Small cost, but it permanently adds about 40 lines of manual layout code.
design_lesson: When a platform primitive has inconsistent timing or support across engines, agents rationally route around it. Interop on behaviour, not just presence, plus clear docs on how it composes with script scroll adjustments, would let the declarative feature win.

pattern: sticky element without z-index painted under positioned content (stacking context)
summary: The mobile bottom nav was position:sticky with no z-index, so the map page's positioned overlays (Leaflet panes and controls at z-index 4-5) and sticky table heads painted over it. The user reported it. The agent first wrote a regression test that hit-tests each nav link with shadowRoot.elementFromPoint at 375px width, confirmed it failed, then fixed it in one edit with isolation:isolate on <main> plus z-index:1 on the nav.
cost_estimate: Fix itself took about 1 minute and 2 edits. The whole session ran about 6 minutes and roughly 45 tool calls, mostly test-port collisions and flaky-suite reruns. 10.5k output tokens.
design_lesson: Stacking is global and implicit: a component can't declare 'I'm a top-level chrome layer' without knowing every other z-index on the page. Top-layer or explicit layering primitives, and devtools or lint warnings for sticky or fixed elements without their own stacking context, would make this hard to get wrong.

pattern: table cell allowed to wrap; ellipsis in table cells needs the width:100%/max-width:0 hack
summary: An earlier design left the packet table's Summary cell as white-space:normal with overflow-wrap:anywhere. In narrow layouts rows grew to 2-3 lines, and the user sent a screenshot. The agent switched to text-overflow:ellipsis, which only works in an auto-layout table cell with the non-obvious 'width:100%; max-width:0' trick. The regression test needed three iterations (row lookup, then a narrower viewport), and the agent removed a no-horizontal-scroll assertion on the way.
cost_estimate: About 35 tool calls, about 7k output tokens, about 5 min. Three test iterations, two of them failure-screenshot reads.
design_lesson: text-overflow on table cells depends on undocumented sizing tricks; a direct primitive (for example a line-clamp or 'shrink-to-fit-column' that works in tables) would make the robust choice the obvious one.

pattern: text-overflow: ellipsis on an inline element has no effect
summary: Adding a '2.0 km away' prefix to contact rows made the phone-width layout test fail with horizontal overflow. The agent found the existing `.row-sub` span already had ellipsis styles that had never worked because it was an inline span; it made it and `.preview` block-level. A latent bug from earlier agent-written CSS, caught by a layout test.
cost_estimate: ~3 tool calls, under 1 minute
design_lesson: Properties that silently do nothing in the wrong context (text-overflow on inline boxes) give no signal; devtools/lint warnings for no-op declarations would catch it.

pattern: 100dvh + calc() height guesses on a scrolling document under Android Chrome's collapsible top controls
summary: The app shell used min-height:100dvh with sticky header/nav, and chat/node pages guessed their height with calc(100dvh - 6.5rem). On Android Chrome (dynamic toolbar, installed-app view) the document still scrolled, the composer sat partly under the bottom nav, and desktop Settings scrolled the sidebar. User reported it; the agent first tried height:100dvh;overflow:hidden on the host, then switched to position:fixed;inset:0 with html/body overflow:hidden + overscroll-behavior:none and <main> as the only scroller, plus moving packets-page IntersectionObserver/scroll anchoring off window.
cost_estimate: ~6 min, ~45 tool calls in round 1 (11:53-11:59); session total ~244 events, 7.2M cache-read tokens across both rounds
design_lesson: There is no single obvious, documented primitive for 'make the app exactly the visible viewport and never scroll the document'; the vh/svh/dvh/lvh + interactive-widget + fixed-positioning matrix forces agents to guess and verify on real devices.

pattern: white-space: pre-wrap on a container renders template-literal whitespace
summary: Chat bubbles had a large leading indent because pre-wrap was set on the .bubble element, so the whitespace/newlines of the Lit template were rendered. Found by a QA subagent driving the app in real Chrome (a 3.5 h, 172-tool-call pass); fixed by applying pre-wrap only to the text span.
cost_estimate: QA agent overall 221k tokens / 172 tool uses / ~3.5h (6 bugs); this fix small
design_lesson: Whitespace handling that depends on how markup is authored is invisible in source review; only rendering reveals it.

pattern: devtools MCP cannot attach to user's existing Chrome; agent hand-writes CDP client
summary: The chrome-devtools MCP launched its own browser profile and could not attach to the user's Chrome on port 4336, so the agent wrote raw CDP WebSocket scripts (cdp.mjs, ble-retry.mjs, drive.mjs) including shadow-DOM-piercing text/click helpers; one 'fill' hit the Messages nav link instead of the textarea.
cost_estimate: ~3 custom scripts, ~20 tool calls over the session
design_lesson: n/a (tooling contrast)

pattern: long-running subagents and /loop polling with nudges
summary: The orchestrator waited hours on subagents (Phase 12, QA, conformance ran ~3 h; a test-fix agent appeared stuck waiting on its own background run) via repeated ScheduleWakeup polling and SendMessage nudges ('Status check after 3 hours: please wrap up').
cost_estimate: Dozens of wake-up turns over ~8h
design_lesson: n/a (tooling contrast)

pattern: compound shell commands containing git refused by the worktree isolation checker; agent must split into plain commands
summary: In this batch, 33 tool calls across 17 of 20 sessions were refused because a compound command named git 'in a form too complex to verify' or used git -C against the main checkout. Each refusal costs a retry with split commands. Merges into main were often impossible from the worktree, which led to multi-turn handoffs to the user.
cost_estimate: About 33 refused calls in the batch, each followed by 1-3 retry calls. Several sessions needed extra user turns to land work.
design_lesson: Not a web API, but the same lesson applies: when a safety layer rejects a call, it should say exactly which form is acceptable, so agents don't trial-and-error their way there.

pattern: confident wrong root cause; real cause was DNS AAAA '::' routing ssh to localhost
summary: Asked why ssh reported a changed host key for argus, the agent concluded the full-name known_hosts entry was stale from a reinstall. The user said the server was new; further digging showed the Firewalla answered AAAA '::' for argus, so ssh over IPv6 reached the Mac's own sshd and its key. It was fixed by rebooting argus so the router learned its IPv6 address.
cost_estimate: ~45 min wall clock, ~150 events
design_lesson: Contrast case: a plausible-sounding first diagnosis without checking all address families; not web-specific.

api: DOM async rendering (<dialog> + Lit) / app state loading
pattern: flaky UI test from reading async-loaded state when a dialog opens; misdiagnosed across sessions
summary: ChannelsModel.details() (added in session_01LUgj4) read only the in-memory channel list, so opening the details <dialog> soon after the chat opened sometimes showed 'no longer stored'. session_014deW blamed it on the dialog's open flag flipping before Lit rendered and made the test wait for a field. session_01Qczhzo's subagent hit it 'every time' after adding a command. This session looped the test 20x (15/20 failed), checked the failure screenshot, and fixed details() to fall back to IndexedDB. The rest of the flake was a Vitest port clash.
cost_estimate: This session: about 75 tool calls and 3 loops of 20 test runs, roughly 14k output tokens over about 17 min. Across sessions the test was flagged as flaky in at least 6 of the 20 batch sessions (01LMjB, 014deW, 01U9PR, 01BadQ, 01SRNh, 01Qczh).
design_lesson: UI state that loads asynchronously needs an observable 'ready' signal (or an API that awaits it), so that 'dialog is open' and 'content is ready' can't be confused.

pattern: flaky test reads dialog content before async render completes
summary: A 'shows channel details (key, hash, slot) from the chat header' browser test failed intermittently in at least four sessions of this batch (011pjNMQ, 01MZb8x6, 014C6Tis, 01TGngzA). Each session spent reruns deciding it was unrelated; only 01TGngzA identified a cause (it reads a dialog field before it renders), and nobody fixed it.
cost_estimate: 2-6 extra full/partial web-suite runs per session across 4 sessions (~1-3 min each)
design_lesson: Rendering that completes asynchronously with no standard 'rendered/settled' signal invites check-before-ready races; an observable settle point makes tests deterministic.

pattern: removeEventListener called with a different function reference than was added
summary: In waitForAdvertisement the agent registered resolve directly as the 'advertisementreceived' listener, but removed onAdvert (a variable that held the same resolve, not a wrapper) in finally. It caught this in a follow-up edit 12 seconds later and switched to a single onAdvert wrapper used for the timer, add and remove. An AbortController was already in scope for watchAdvertisements, so passing {signal} to addEventListener would have avoided the identity bookkeeping entirely.
cost_estimate: 1 extra edit, under 1 minute
design_lesson: Listener removal by function identity is fragile. Making AbortSignal the default teardown idiom in docs and examples, e.g. addEventListener(type, fn, {signal}), removes a whole class of mismatch bugs.

pattern: test asserted toggle state while button was still disabled (async save in flight)
summary: A new browser test for the favourite star toggle passed alone but failed in the full parallel run ('timed out waiting for unstarred'). The button is disabled while the radio save is in flight, so the second click landed on a disabled button. Fixed by waiting for aria-pressed and !disabled before the next step.
cost_estimate: ~3 tool calls, ~1.5 min, 3 extra full web test runs
design_lesson: Clicks on disabled buttons are silently dropped; an observable 'interaction ignored' signal (or test helpers that fail loudly) would avoid timing-dependent flakes.

pattern: wrong root cause: assumed dialog.open flips before render; patched the test, not the app
summary: Ping work hit the channel-details test failure. It failed on every full run but passed alone. The agent read the test and decided <dialog>.open becomes true before Lit renders the fields. It changed the test to wait for a field to exist and committed that as the fix. The real cause, an app-level race reading unloaded channel state, survived and was found later in session_01A7jk.
cost_estimate: About 8 tool calls (roughly 3 full web-suite runs), about 5 min. The larger cost was downstream: the flake persisted into 3+ later sessions.
design_lesson: Clear, documented guarantees about when declarative rendering has committed to the DOM (an updateComplete-style contract) would discourage 'wait longer' fixes that hide state races.

pattern: IndexedDB is origin-global: parallel test iframes share and delete each other's databases
summary: Browser tests ran in parallel iframes of one origin; every harness used the same emulator key, so all files shared 'meshcore-web:<key>' DBs and cleanup() deleted every meshcore-web:* database, including ones open in other iframes. Earlier sessions had worked around it by disabling fileParallelism (21s suite). A reviewer agent diagnosed it and the fix was a hand-rolled prefixing IDBFactory wrapper; the first run after the change still failed a test that read the unscoped global indexedDB ('expected 0 to be greater than 10').
cost_estimate: Reviewer subagent + ~6 orchestrator tool calls for the fix, ~20k tokens; suite 21s -> ~5s once fixed
design_lesson: Storage APIs that support explicit namespacing/partitioning (or a per-context test origin) would make isolation the default instead of a hand-built IDBFactory proxy.

pattern: no per-database size API; estimate by full cursor scan
summary: User asked to show the IndexedDB log database size per known radio. There is no API for per-database size (navigator.storage.estimate() is origin-wide), so a subagent wrote approxValueBytes() heuristics (strings 2 bytes/char, numbers 8 …) and a cursor pass over every store of every radio DB, plus a StorageModel with coalescing/refresh logic, and labelled results '≈'.
cost_estimate: two implementation subagents (~5 min each); session 66k output tokens, 9.9M cache-read; new db-stats.ts + storage-model.ts + 3 test files
design_lesson: Storage quotas are exposed only per origin; a per-database (or per-bucket) usage figure would replace hundreds of lines of approximate byte-counting code.

pattern: indexedDB.open() silently creates a missing/deleted database
summary: The first stats helper opened each radio's DB to count records; when indexedDB.databases() was unavailable it 'opened with the same migrations', and a stats pass racing a delete could recreate the just-deleted database. Found by the second subagent while adding a Remove button; fixed by aborting the upgrade transaction so stats never create a DB.
cost_estimate: part of a ~5 min subagent run; a few tool calls plus a new test
design_lesson: An open() that creates-on-miss has a dangerous side effect for read-only callers; an explicit open-existing-only option would make the safe path the default.

pattern: git worktree without node_modules resolves workspace package from main checkout
summary: In a fresh worktree, web typecheck resolved @meshcore-web/core through the parent checkout's node_modules symlink and saw stale core source ('has no exported member'). Agent diagnosed after several typecheck attempts, ran npm install, and wrote a memory note.
cost_estimate: ~5 tool calls, ~2 min
design_lesson: n/a (tooling contrast)

pattern: installed PWA leaves unthemed system-bar area: missing viewport-fit=cover + safe-area insets
summary: The agent-built PWA (session PJZj) shipped without viewport-fit=cover, safe-area padding or a dark theme-color, so the installed Android app showed a white bar under the app switcher. A human user filed the issue with the exact fix. A subagent added viewport-fit=cover, env(safe-area-inset-*) padding on header/nav/main/toasts, light+dark theme-color metas; it could not verify on a device and noted the manifest has no widely supported dark background.
cost_estimate: 1 subagent run (shared with #4/#14), ~153 lines changed across 14 files; fix unverified
design_lesson: Opt-in edge-to-edge behaviour (viewport-fit) plus untestable-in-headless installed-app chrome means agents can't see the bug; safer defaults or an emulatable installed-mode would help.

api: Popover API / interestfor / CSS anchor positioning
pattern: agent retrieved guidance for new declarative API (popover=hint + interestfor + anchor positioning) but hand-built the old JS way
summary: Before building field tooltips, the agent ran the modern-web-guidance skill. It returned the 'interest-triggered-tooltips' guide recommending popover="hint", interestfor and anchor positioning. The agent instead built a manual popover: showPopover() from Lit updated(), JS getBoundingClientRect positioning with flip-above logic, a window keydown listener for Escape, and a hide timer. The transcript gives no reason. A screenshot check then showed byte tooltips covering the next hex row, so it re-anchored them below the hex dump, which is the kind of placement anchor positioning fallbacks handle declaratively.
cost_estimate: Guidance lookup was 3 tool calls, about 3k tokens of guide. Building the manual tooltip, its test and the screenshot iteration took about 7 minutes and roughly 30 tool calls. 67k output tokens for the session overall (much of it git and permission friction).
design_lesson: Even when an agent is handed the modern declarative pattern, it falls back to imperative positioning, most likely because interestfor and anchor positioning aren't Baseline and it's unclear how they behave across shadow roots. Clear Baseline status, fallbacks and shadow-DOM guidance in the guide itself would make the new API the default choice.

pattern: single-point SVG line path renders nothing; points outside a fixed x-domain clipped
summary: The d3-shape line charts the subagent built drew nothing when a series had only one time bin, because a path with a single point has no visible stroke. Fixed x-domains also cut off bins that started before the domain on round boundaries. The orchestrator caught both by writing a throwaway vitest-browser screenshot test and looking at the PNGs in light and dark. It added a circle marker for one-point series and widened the domain to the data extent. No unit test had caught it.
cost_estimate: Screenshot loop of 4 renders plus 3 image reads, about 7 minutes including a 5-minute hang from `vitest -w` (watch mode). Images are expensive in context.
design_lesson: Visual-only failures (an invisible mark) pass DOM-level tests. Agents need cheap rendering checks such as 'is anything painted for this element?', or accessible-chart semantics, to verify graphics without screenshots.

pattern: querySelector does not pierce nested shadow roots in tests
summary: After moving the path page into a nested <mc-node-path> tab inside the node page's shadow root, test selectors stopped matching. The agent checked whether the test harness pierces nested shadow roots, found it can't, and rewrote/simplified selectors.
cost_estimate: ~4 tool calls, ~1 minute
design_lesson: A standard deep/piercing query (or a test-oriented equivalent) for composed trees would avoid every component refactor breaking selectors.

pattern: no way to observe that a stream reader has consumed data, so tests slept
summary: A Web Serial transport test used setTimeout(5) to wait for the reader loop to consume a partial frame before disconnecting; if timing slipped the test silently stopped testing the case. Fix relied on a non-obvious streams property: with highWaterMark 0, the underlying source's pull() fires exactly when the consumer awaits read() on an empty queue.
cost_estimate: 1 edit; small
design_lesson: Streams semantics (when pull() fires, how backpressure maps to reader state) need to be documented as observable contracts, not left to spec-reading.

pattern: test runner started in watch mode and hung
summary: While checking whether a failing messaging test was flaky, the agent ran vitest in a form that started watch mode; the command hung for ~10 minutes until timeout before the agent killed it and ran the file directly. Separately, several sessions hit browser-test port clashes from concurrent sessions.
cost_estimate: ~10 min wall-clock (02:56:43 to 03:06:44), 1 hung tool call
design_lesson: Tools whose default mode is interactive/long-lived are hostile to agents; non-interactive defaults when no TTY is present avoid silent hangs.

api: Vitest browser mode / Node net (port binding)
pattern: fixed default test-server port clashes across parallel agent sessions; IPv4-only repro missed ::1 binding
summary: Parallel sessions on one machine each ran Vitest browser mode, which binds a default port 63315 with strictPort inherited from the dev-server config. Runs failed with 'Port 63315 is already in use'. Sessions coped with retry loops (01U9PR), waiting on the other PID (019ipp), retries (01Emyn) or --api.port (01Qczh subagents). This session set test.api.strictPort:false. Its first 'port held' repro was invalid because a Python holder bound IPv4 127.0.0.1 while Vite bound [::1].
cost_estimate: This session: about 20 tool calls (roughly 5k tokens) on the port issue. The issue recurred in at least 5 of the 20 batch sessions.
design_lesson: Tools should default to picking a free port and should report the actual bound address family; 'localhost' resolving to ::1 vs 127.0.0.1 is a recurring trap.

pattern: parallel agents colliding on test port and merge conflicts
summary: Five-to-seven parallel subagents repeatedly collided on the vitest browser API port (orchestrator learned '--browser.api.port does not work', use --api.port), and overlapping edits (two path resolvers, app.paths name clash) forced aborted cherry-picks and extra rebase agents. Auto-mode classifier also blocked git push until the user re-confirmed.
cost_estimate: Extra integration agent runs (2+ rebases), ~1h of orchestration
design_lesson: n/a (tooling contrast)

pattern: guessing CLI flag names for test-runner port when parallel agents collide
summary: Several parallel agent sessions ran browser tests at once and collided on vitest's default browser API port 63315. The agents retried, read the configs, used lsof and ps to find the other job, then guessed --browser.api.port (no effect) before finding that --api.port works. Another session used a sleep-20 retry loop instead. This recurred in Y7su, C3Yb, M6cM and Peup.
cost_estimate: About 6-8 tool calls and 1-2 minutes per occurrence. 4 sessions affected.
design_lesson: Tools run concurrently by agents should default to an ephemeral or free port (or strictPort:false) and print the exact flag to override it.

pattern: flaky browser test investigation by repeated full-suite runs
summary: A messaging browser test failed intermittently on the first full run after each change. The agent looped full suites, cleared the Vite cache to reproduce a 'cold' failure, and checked history, ~10 full web-suite runs, before landing anyway and flagging it. Also hit a vitest browser API port collision with another session and Vite server.fs 'Access denied' for a screenshot path outside the root.
cost_estimate: ~10 full suite runs, ~15 tool calls, ~10 min across 17:03-17:35
design_lesson: Test runners should report the root cause of flakes (e.g. which async state was pending) rather than pass/fail.

pattern: manifest icon purpose 'any' only, so Android shrinks it inside a white shape (no maskable variant)
summary: The PWA manifest from earlier work shipped only purpose:'any' icons, so the Android launcher shrank the icon inside a white circle. The user noticed and asked the agent to search the web for the fix. The agent did one WebSearch on maskable icons and the safe zone, generated maskable SVG/PNG variants (artwork inside a 40% radius safe circle), updated the manifest and app name, and checked a circle-masked preview rendered with Playwright.
cost_estimate: About 4 minutes, 1 web search and roughly 25 tool calls. 10k output tokens.
design_lesson: Installability checks pass without a maskable icon, and the platform quietly letterboxes it. A manifest validator or install-time warning ('no maskable icon; Android will shrink it') would catch this when the manifest is written.

pattern: wrong mental model of getDevices() availability/persistence without persistent-permissions flag
summary: User reported reload auto-reconnect failing with 'No previously allowed Bluetooth device'. Agent asserted navigator.bluetooth.getDevices() 'only exists with the persistent-permissions flag'; user replied getDevices exists without the flag. Agent then claimed without the flag getDevices only returns devices picked 'since the page loaded' and wrote a user-facing error message on that basis; user then reloaded and it reconnected fine, so agent reversed a third time: grants without the flag are in-memory per browser session (survive reload, lost on Chrome restart). Took 4 user round-trips, a console diagnostic script, a background web-research subagent; the shipped message text still says 'after the page reloaded'.
cost_estimate: ~5 user turns over ~5h wall-clock (20:57 to 01:43, mostly user idle); ~45 tool calls incl. a web-research subagent; session 38k output tokens, 3.4M cache-read
design_lesson: A method whose return value silently depends on a hidden flag and an undocumented in-memory vs persisted grant lifetime is undiagnosable; expose the permission's persistence (e.g. a 'persisted' attribute or permissions.query state) and document grant lifetime explicitly.

pattern: assumed getDevices() absent without flag; encoded wrong model in code, tests and README
summary: Asked to make the Reconnect button skip the chooser, the agent concluded Chrome hides getDevices() behind a flag and only narrowed requestDevice() with an exact-name filter. It baked the assumption into the commit message, README ('no getDevices(), e.g. Chrome without the persistent-permissions flag') and a test named 'without getDevices(), Reconnect shows a chooser…'. A later session (016p7fHi) showed getDevices() exists without the flag and returns in-session grants, so the real reason was lost grants after browser restart.
cost_estimate: ~40 tool calls, ~4 min wall-clock; 17k output tokens; misdiagnosis propagated into the follow-up session
design_lesson: Feature detection ('getDevices' in navigator.bluetooth) can't reveal partial behaviour; APIs gated by flags should either be absent or fully behave, and MDN/spec should state grant persistence semantics.

pattern: can't determine whether a gated API (getDevices, persistent BLE permissions) is enabled by default; docs are stale
summary: Asked whether Bluetooth could reconnect after a reload without user interaction, the agent searched the web. It found only 2020-era sources saying getDevices() and persistent permissions were behind chrome://flags, and couldn't confirm current default status. It built getDevices() matching by stored device.id, plus a watchAdvertisements wait before gatt.connect() because 'Chrome only connects to a device it has seen recently'. It shipped with a caveat to enable a flag if the chooser still appears. Everything was tested only against a mock, never real hardware.
cost_estimate: Research took 1 web search and about 1 minute. The implementation ran about 8 minutes and roughly 40 tool calls (mock BLE, transport, tests). 41k output tokens across the session (includes later rebases). The behaviour on real devices is still unknown.
design_lesson: Agents need a machine-readable, current answer to 'is this API and its permission persistence on by default in browser X?'. BCD/chromestatus coverage for permission-persistence behaviour, plus a runtime-queryable capability (e.g. permissions.query for 'bluetooth' reporting persistence), would replace guesswork about flags.

pattern: reply timeout started before the GATT write resolved; OS pairing/PIN dialog during first write caused timeout
summary: The client started its 5 s reply timeout before the write completed. On a first BLE connect the OS pairing PIN dialog blocks the write, so the first command timed out and the client concluded the device was very old firmware, losing device info. The conformance-review agent moved the timer start to after the write resolves, with a 60 s cap on the write.
cost_estimate: Found in conformance-review subagent; small fix
design_lesson: Implicit, user-visible side effects (pairing UI) hidden inside writeValue() should be explicit in the API (e.g. a separate pairing step or event) so timeouts can be reasoned about.

pattern: empty chooser reported as 'User cancelled' NotFoundError; app hid the cause
summary: User said 'BLE connection failed'. The app's connect page only showed 'BLE connect failed'. The agent wrote a CDP script to wrap navigator.bluetooth calls and re-click Connect; the trace showed requestDevice rejecting with NotFoundError 'User cancelled the requestDevice() chooser.' even though the user saw an empty list. The agent went digging into firmware advertising code until the user realised the radio was connected to their phone and so not advertising.
cost_estimate: ~12 tool calls, ~4 min wall clock (11:47-11:51), ~15k tokens incl. CDP instrumentation script
design_lesson: requestDevice() should distinguish 'no matching devices found' from 'user dismissed', and app/agent-visible errors should carry that cause.

pattern: back-to-back write-without-response on a GATT characteristic merges frames on device
summary: The transport agent's BLE transport defaulted to writes without response. A later protocol-conformance review agent found nRF52 firmware treats everything in its RX buffer as one frame, so back-to-back unacknowledged writes can merge into one corrupt frame; it switched the default to writeValueWithResponse (as meshcore.js does) with an opt-out.
cost_estimate: Found in conformance-review subagent; 1 transport change + test update
design_lesson: The API gives no signal about message boundaries or flow control for write-without-response; documenting that GATT writes are not framed/queued semantics would prevent this.

pattern: async-only SubtleCrypto forces a parallel synchronous SHA-256/HMAC implementation for reactive/computed code
summary: Region keys are SHA256('#name')[0..16] and transport codes are HMAC-SHA256 truncated. The app has async versions (regionKey and calcTransportCode in packet.ts, built on crypto.subtle). The plan and implementation for a reactive keys signal and per-packet region matching used sync variants (regionKeySync, sha256Sync, transportCodeSync from emulator/crypto-sync.ts), because computed signals and render paths can't await. The plan cites existing precedent (app/reactions.ts already imports crypto-sync). That means two crypto implementations to maintain, plus research tokens spent working out which one to use.
cost_estimate: Hard to isolate. It shows up in planning and subagent prompts (several hundred tokens of explanation) and in an ongoing maintenance cost; it's not a debugging loop.
design_lesson: Offering a synchronous digest and HMAC for small inputs (or a sync worker-friendly variant) would remove the need for apps to ship hand-rolled crypto just to use hashes in synchronous/reactive code.

pattern: WebAuthn expected origin derived from request Host/Origin headers instead of configuration
summary: The N5b subagent implemented passkey login with a sameOrigin helper that accepted the clientData Origin whenever it matched the request's Host header, and the WebSocket Origin check likewise trusted Host. A read-only security-review subagent flagged that a non-browser relayer controls both headers, so only rpIdHash was really checked: with the default rpId 'localhost' any page on any localhost port, or any subdomain of the rpId, could relay an assertion and get a 30-day token. Fixed by deriving allowed origins only from --origin/TLS names, refusing non-loopback binds without --origin/--rp-id and rejecting IP-literal rpIds.
cost_estimate: one extra review subagent plus a hardening subagent (~30 min wall clock 00:35-01:09); subagent token counts not visible in this transcript
design_lesson: WebAuthn's origin/rpId model (rpId scoped to host not port, subdomains share credentials) is easy to verify wrongly server-side; specs and libraries should make 'expected origin comes from config, never the request' the default and document the localhost/port caveat prominently.

pattern: WebCrypto Ed25519 only signs from a 32-byte seed, not the firmware's 64-byte expanded key
summary: The packet-codec agent built Ed25519 sign/verify and X25519 on crypto.subtle, then discovered WebCrypto can only import the 32-byte seed. Private keys exported from real MeshCore hardware are the 64-byte expanded form, so the app can decrypt with them but cannot sign adverts. Surfaced as an open question to the orchestrator.
cost_estimate: Discovered within Phase 3a subagent; left as limitation
design_lesson: Key-import formats should cover common real-world encodings (e.g. expanded Ed25519 private keys) or fail with an explicit, documented error.

pattern: SubtleCrypto lacks AES-ECB so a cipher had to be hand-written
summary: The protocol uses AES-128-ECB with zero padding; SubtleCrypto offers no ECB mode, so the orchestrator instructed a subagent to implement and test a pure-TS AES-128 block cipher against FIPS-197 vectors and an openssl-built packet.
cost_estimate: Part of the Phase 3a packet-codec subagent; AES + test vectors maybe 10-20k tokens
design_lesson: Exposing primitive block-cipher operations (or a documented escape hatch) avoids agents re-implementing crypto from scratch.

pattern: promise-only crypto breaks deterministic synchronous simulation, forcing a ~300-line BigInt crypto twin
summary: The emulator/virtual-mesh agent needed hashing and signing inside a synchronous, manually clocked simulation. It measured that in Node WebCrypto promises only resolve after a macrotask (0 of 50 SHA-256 digests done by setTimeout(0)), so it wrote emulator/crypto-sync.ts: SHA-256/512, HMAC, Ed25519 and X25519 in BigInt (~300 lines), cross-tested against packet/crypto and RFC vectors. Side effect: the sync version can sign with expanded keys, which WebCrypto cannot.
cost_estimate: Large share of the Phase 3c subagent (~300 LOC + tests); likely tens of thousands of tokens
design_lesson: A synchronous (or microtask-resolving) digest/sign API for small inputs would remove the need for agents to duplicate an entire crypto library to test deterministically.

pattern: cannot update a branch checked out in another worktree
summary: Agent pushed HEAD:main from the worktree, then tried 'git fetch origin main:main' to update local main, which git refuses because main is checked out in the primary worktree; the worktree guard also refused python text naming git. User later changed the workflow (session 012Q).
cost_estimate: 2-3 tool calls
design_lesson: n/a (tooling contrast)

pattern: nested setTimeout clamped to >=4ms after 5 levels slows simulated event chains
summary: The mock Web Bluetooth device delivered each GATT notification via setTimeout(0) scheduled from the previous timer callback, and test 'until' loops polled with setTimeout(1). Chromium's nested-timer clamping made each step >=4ms, so mocked BLE connect took ~110ms vs 65ms for serial. Reviewer agent identified it; fix was a MessageChannel-based nextTask().
cost_estimate: Part of one reviewer report; ~2 edits; small
design_lesson: A first-class 'yield to next task' primitive (e.g. scheduler.yield / postTask) avoids folklore like MessageChannel hacks to dodge timer clamping.

pattern: interactive-widget=resizes-content shrinks layout under keyboard; no way to detect keyboard, focus used as proxy
summary: In the first fix the agent added interactive-widget=resizes-content so the keyboard would not cover the composer. The user then reported portrait messages still scrolling on Android: with the keyboard up the layout is only ~350px, smaller than the fixed chrome plus the chat's 20rem min-height. The agent measured layouts at short heights in the headless test browser (console output was suppressed, so it re-encoded numbers as failing-test messages), then added a TypingController that treats 'a text field has focus' as 'keyboard is up' and hides nav/headers. It was never verified on a real phone.
cost_estimate: round 2: ~7 min (12:05-12:12), ~60 tool calls including throwaway measurement tests; regression caused by agent's own round-1 change
design_lesson: A portable, testable signal for 'on-screen keyboard is showing and how tall it is' (VirtualKeyboard API is Chromium-only and not emulated in headless tests) would let agents avoid focus-as-proxy heuristics and catch regressions without a physical device.

pattern: passed a path-like name to a.download; browser silently flattens '/' to '_'
summary: The app names files opened from a granted folder by their relative path (e.g. runs/2026-07/a.zpcr) and the download helper passed that straight to a.download. Chrome doesn't reject or strip directory parts; it silently replaces the slashes with underscores, so users got very long filenames. The user reported it; the agent added a downloadName() basename helper and a CDP Page.downloadWillBegin check of suggestedFilename.
cost_estimate: Small: ~8 tool calls and about 2 minutes for the fix and a CDP-based test, roughly 6k tokens.
design_lesson: The download attribute silently sanitizes illegal characters. A warning in the console, or a documented 'basename only' contract, would surface the mistake when the code is written rather than when a user sees the file.

pattern: uncertain whether interactive controls inside <summary> toggle the <details>
summary: Moving a panel header that holds checkboxes and a Clear button into a <summary>, the agent first wrote click handlers with preventDefault to stop the panel folding. Before testing it reversed itself: a button or checkbox inside a summary is its own activation target, and preventDefault would have broken the checkboxes. It then confirmed with a one-off CDP script that the checkbox flips while the panel stays open.
cost_estimate: ~2 edits plus a ~6-call ad-hoc verification script; ~1 min, ~5k tokens
design_lesson: The summary activation-target rule is subtle and goes unstated in most docs, so agents hedge with defensive preventDefault that would break things; MDN-level docs on nested interactive content in <summary> would remove the guesswork.

pattern: used a newer built-in (findLast) not in the project's TS lib target
summary: The agent used Array.prototype.findLast in a test. The tests passed at runtime, but core's tsc failed with TS2550 because the project's lib predates ES2023. It had half-suspected this earlier, and replaced the call with [...arr].reverse().find(...).
cost_estimate: 2-3 tool calls, under 1 min, ~2K tokens
design_lesson: Agents default to the newest built-ins; a per-project baseline signal (e.g. Baseline year in tsconfig, or lint) surfaced at authoring time avoids the round-trip.

pattern: fr unit inside min() makes the whole declaration invalid and it is silently dropped
summary: To cap well-matrix columns at 19px while keeping them flexible, the agent wrote grid-template-columns: auto repeat(var(--cols), minmax(0, min(1fr, var(--wm-cell-max)))). An fr value isn't allowed inside min(), so the browser threw away the whole declaration with no console error. The grid fell back to a single 281px column, and all 96 cells became 281x281. The agent caught it only by writing CDP measurement scripts that read getBoundingClientRect and the computed gridTemplateColumns ('281px'), then switched to minmax(0, 19px).
cost_estimate: About 8 tool calls (4 throwaway CDP measurement scripts) over 13:28-13:30, roughly 3 min. Episode about 12k chars, so about 3k tokens of transcript, plus a dev server and Chrome per script.
design_lesson: An invalid CSS value should raise a diagnostic (a console warning or a CSS.supports-style check in devtools/CDP) instead of failing silently. 'Flexible but capped' tracks need a first-class, obvious spelling (e.g. fr allowed in min/clamp).

pattern: auto track + aspect-ratio feedback loop blows up an empty cell; agent's own measurement showed it but went unnoticed
summary: After the min() fix the agent measured the single-row Biomeme grid as '83px 19px 19px …' and said it was fixed, missing that the auto row-header column had grown to 83px. The user later reported a 'spacing problem' with a screenshot. In a narrow window the empty corner button's auto column grew to 384px: aspect-ratio:1 tied its width to a stretched row height. The agent wrote two more CDP repro scripts that walked computed styles up the ancestor chain, then replaced auto with a fixed minmax(0,19px) track.
cost_estimate: About 11 tool calls over 23:35-23:38 (about 3.5 min), plus one extra user round-trip with a screenshot. About 20k chars of transcript (roughly 5k tokens).
design_lesson: Interactions between intrinsic sizing (auto tracks, stretched rows) and aspect-ratio are hard to predict; a layout-debugging API that explains why a track got its size, or warnings for cyclic percentage/aspect dependencies, would let an agent check layout without screenshots.

pattern: cursor:pointer applied by class rather than by actual interactivity
summary: A previous agent put cursor:pointer on .instrument__panelhead, a class shared by clickable <summary> heads and a non-interactive <div> holding a pulsing 'running' badge. The user reported the false affordance. The fix scoped the rule to summary.instrument__panelhead and recorded a rule in ARCHITECTURE.md to use pointer only on clickable things.
cost_estimate: About 2 minutes, roughly 25 tool calls (mostly grep/sed to locate the rule).
design_lesson: Cursor affordance is decoupled from interactivity semantics: browsers don't give <summary>, role=button or onclick elements a pointer, and nothing stops it on inert elements. Defaulting cursor from role or activation behavior would remove a recurring class of agent (and human) slips.

pattern: role="button" element without pointer cursor
summary: The load-file dropzone, built by an earlier agent, had role="button" and click-to-browse behavior but no cursor:pointer, so only part of it looked clickable. The user reported it, and the agent added cursor:pointer to .dropzone (disabled already overrode it to default). This is the mirror image of the L92 incident in the same batch.
cost_estimate: About 1 minute, 15 tool calls (most of them git/worktree overhead).
design_lesson: Declaring role=button changes semantics for assistive tech but nothing visual, so agents must remember to restate affordances in CSS by hand. A semantics-driven default cursor would make the robust path the default.

pattern: guessed CSS variable names; undefined var() fails silently
summary: When writing new Overview CSS, the agent used design tokens that don't exist (--line, --ink-dim). Undefined custom properties fail silently, so typecheck, tests and the screenshot showed nothing. The agent noticed only by grepping theme.css afterwards. The same grep showed a pre-existing rule already using the undefined --ink-dim, which the agent noted and left unfixed.
cost_estimate: ~6 tool calls, <1 min; low tokens, but the existing silent bug stayed in production
design_lesson: Referencing an undefined custom property with no fallback should be detectable (a devtools/console warning or a @property registry with checks) instead of silently computing to the initial value.

pattern: adding a flex item overflows a fixed narrow-viewport budget; layout regressions invisible without a measuring test
summary: Adding a ninth 'Protocol' tab pushed the header's tightest icon-only collapse level (data-fit=3) 11px past a 480px viewport. A header-fit UI check that measures overflow caught it. The agent first called the failures pre-existing because they also showed on a temp checkout of main. It then wrote a CDP probe script, which needed three attempts to get the harness imports and Chrome profile right, read the header CSS, and tightened the group gaps at that collapse level only.
cost_estimate: ~15:50–15:58 (~8 min), ~30 tool calls incl. a temp main worktree with 2 UI-suite runs and a probe script
design_lesson: Overflow is silent in CSS; a declarative way to detect or forbid overflow (or container-query fallbacks that collapse automatically) would spare agents from measuring layout by script.

pattern: grid item falls into implicit track when column template is narrower than children
summary: The agent made the row button its own grid but declared too few columns, so the description column fell into an implicit grid track and rendered in the wrong place. Nothing errored; the agent found it only by viewing a screenshot, and it fixed the template in the same pass as a popover-overflow fix.
cost_estimate: ~4 tool calls, ~2 min
design_lesson: Silent implicit-track creation gives agents no signal; a dev-mode warning when items overflow the explicit grid would surface it without a screenshot.

pattern: hand-tuning max-height pixel budgets via screenshot loops in a nested grid/scroll layout
summary: Adding a protocol-staging panel to the Device view's fixed grid (rows `1fr minmax(180px, 40%)`), the agent first hid the action buttons inside a scroll container. It then squeezed the files panel to nothing, and went through several screenshot iterations tweaking max-height values (320→200, 240→150→190px). Layout needed retuning twice more later in the session (a compact plate mode, and relaxing caps after a rebase made the column scroll).
cost_estimate: First episode: ~20 tool calls and 4 screenshots (~1.1-1.4k image tokens each), ~3 min. Plus ~6 more screenshot rounds later. Roughly 25-35k tokens in total on layout fitting.
design_lesson: Agents can only check layout by taking screenshots, so magic-number height budgets get tuned by trial and error; intrinsic sizing that 'just fits' and a text-queryable overflow/clipping report (which elements are clipped or scrolled) would replace the image-token loop.

pattern: swapping icon glyphs of different intrinsic width shifts flex layout
summary: The agent swapped the chip's ✕ glyph for a bin glyph when the delete button 'arms'. Its own UI assertion measuring getBoundingClientRect().width showed the chip widened by 4px, shoving the whole file bar. Fixed by giving the glyph a fixed-size box in CSS.
cost_estimate: ~3 tool calls, ~1 min, ~2k tokens
design_lesson: Layout stability is invisible to an agent unless it measures; tooling that flags layout shift on state change (like CLS for interactions) would surface this automatically.

pattern: viewport-width breakpoint used as proxy for "content overflows"
summary: Asked to collapse header labels to icons when the header does not fit, the agent reused a fixed @media (max-width: 599px) breakpoint. It verified only a 390px phone and desktop. The header actually stops fitting at about 780px, so between 600 and 780px it was clipped. The user reported this in the next session, and the fix replaced the media query with JS measurement (useHeaderFit).
cost_estimate: Original session ~49 tool calls, ~6 min; the fix cost a whole follow-up session (~81 tool calls, ~17 min).
design_lesson: CSS has no way to say "use this layout if the content fits, otherwise this one" (no overflow or content-fit query), so agents fall back on a guessed viewport number. A declarative fit/overflow condition would remove the guess.

pattern: hand-positioned dropdown overflows viewport; supported anchor positioning avoided due to cross-browser baseline guidance
summary: A details/summary dropdown reused a rule anchoring its right edge (position:absolute; right:0), so in a left-aligned card the list ran off the left of the viewport. The user caught it from a screenshot; the agent's own screenshot check had missed it. The agent loaded the modern-web-guidance skill, which recommended anchor positioning with position-try-fallbacks, but concluded it 'has no native support yet and needs a CDN polyfill' and switched to a scoped left:0 override. The app is effectively Chromium-only (WebUSB), and a polyfill could be bundled anyway.
cost_estimate: ~25 tool calls, ~4 min wall-clock (18:07-18:11), 2 custom CDP measurement scripts + screenshots + full UI suite; ~8-10k tokens
design_lesson: Overflow-safe anchored popups should be the platform default, and support guidance agents consume should be answerable for the app's actual target browsers, not a generic 'Baseline widely available' rule.

pattern: auto table layout sizes columns from header content (two-digit headers widen columns)
summary: The agent added per-fluor dots inside compact plate-grid <td> cells and checked the result with a screenshot. The user then spotted that columns 10–12 were wider than 1–9: under table-layout:auto, the two-digit header plus 8px of padding widened those columns, so dots wrapped differently. The fix was table-layout:fixed with a 24px header width and no horizontal header padding, verified by measuring every cell over CDP (all 24x24).
cost_estimate: The fix turn took about 3 minutes (18:58–19:01) and 16 tool calls, including a custom CDP measuring script. The original feature turn took about 8 minutes and roughly 70 tool calls, and its screenshot check missed the asymmetry.
design_lesson: Layout that silently depends on content width (auto table layout) is easy to miss in a screenshot. A queryable layout check, or a lint for content-sized grids meant to be uniform, would surface it; agents need measurable invariants, not visual inspection.

pattern: per-cell highlight border under border-collapse loses conflict resolution to neighbour
summary: Earlier agent-written CSS highlighted loaded plate wells by tinting each cell's border inside a `border-collapse: collapse` table. Under the collapsing-border conflict rules, on a colour-only tie the left/top cell wins, so the highlighted well's left edge was drawn in the neighbour's grey. The user reported it with a screenshot; the agent diagnosed it from the spec rule and switched the grid to separate borders.
cost_estimate: Fix itself cheap: ~15 tool calls, ~4 min, ~15k tokens incl. 3 screenshots. The original bug shipped unnoticed until the user saw it.
design_lesson: Implicit, order-dependent conflict resolution (collapsed borders) silently drops a declared style; a non-collapsing per-element primitive (outline/inset ring) or a devtools warning when a declared border loses would make the intent hard to misuse.

pattern: text-overflow:ellipsis needs overflow:hidden + white-space:nowrap + constrained width; one label missed the trio
summary: The user reported that long fluorophore names wrapped and grew the target chips instead of being elided. The .chanchip__dye sublabel was missing the overflow/white-space/text-overflow trio that the main label had. The agent added the four properties, but its uishot sample had only short names, so the fix was never visually reproduced.
cost_estimate: About 12 tool calls, about 2 min, cheap.
design_lesson: Ellipsis takes three cooperating properties plus a width constraint. A single shorthand (e.g. line-clamp / text-wrap style) is harder to half-apply.

pattern: matched DOM text against CSS-transformed rendering (text-transform: uppercase) instead of textContent
summary: The agent wrote a uitest that looked up .alf table columns as cell(r,'STAGE'), cell(r,'HOLD') and so on, which matches how the headers looked in its screenshot. The markup says 'Stage'/'Hold' and CSS uppercases it, so head.indexOf('STAGE') returned -1 and the step-duration and read-index checks failed. The agent noticed from the test output and switched to a case-insensitive lookup.
cost_estimate: ~3 min wall clock (20:17:17 failure to 20:20:17 fix), 1 extra full UI-suite run (~2 min), ~3 tool calls, ~2k tokens
design_lesson: Agents work from screenshots, so what they see and what DOM text APIs return can differ silently (textContent ignores text-transform, while innerText applies it). Docs or devtools should make that difference obvious.

pattern: measuring layout by toggling live styles kills CSS transitions
summary: To collapse header labels exactly when they stop fitting, and animate it, the agent wrote a JS hook. The hook writes data-fit levels, reads the layout back, and sets per-label max-width (because width:auto cannot be transitioned). Its measuring probe set transition:none on the live header, and a first-pass flag re-armed whenever the effect re-ran. Together these made every tab switch snap instead of animate. The agent found this itself by writing six CDP scripts that sampled element widths each frame and listed document animations, then fixed it by moving the flag into a ref.
cost_estimate: About 25 tool calls and ~9 min (12:52-13:01) on the hook and its animation debugging, including 6 throwaway probe scripts (anim..anim6.mjs). The result is a 153-line useHeaderFit.ts for what is conceptually "collapse if overflowing".
design_lesson: Measuring "would this fit at level N?" needs a side-effect-free layout query (or animatable intrinsic sizes such as transitions to width:auto), so that code does not have to mutate live styles and fight its own transitions.

pattern: white-space: pre + overflow-x: auto hides trailing UI off-screen; agent's screenshot verification missed it
summary: Asked to do the pltd XML view, the agent found it already implemented and 'verified' it in the browser via Chrome DevTools MCP clicks and screenshots, then moved on. The user then reported the root node's disclosure triangle and 'N children' count were not visible. Cause: .decoded__xml used white-space: pre; overflow-x: auto, so long attribute lists pushed the controls past the right edge. Fixed with pre-wrap + word-break.
cost_estimate: ~15 DevTools MCP calls for the first (missed) verification, ~10 more for the fix; ~20 min wall clock incl. user wait
design_lesson: Content clipped by horizontal overflow is invisible to screenshot-based checks; tools or APIs that report 'interactive element is outside the visible scrollport' would help agents notice it.

pattern: assumed scrollWidth > clientWidth detects overflow on a non-scrolling flex container
summary: The agent's new header-fit test asserted overflow via scrollWidth, then checked whether the test failed with the fix reverted. It didn't: in a plain non-scrolling flex row, overflowing children paint outside the box without growing the container's scrollWidth, so that half of the check could never fire. The agent switched to comparing the trailing element's right edge, then to the one child that is a scroll container (.app__views with overflow-x:auto). It then ran a sed loop over viewport widths, which hit the tool timeout (exit 143), to pick a stable width of 480px.
cost_estimate: 15:26–15:35 (~9 min), ~12 tool calls, 4 revert/re-run cycles of the UI suite (~55-110s each) plus a timed-out width sweep
design_lesson: There is no direct 'is this element overflowing/clipped' query; an explicit overflow-detection API (or consistent scrollWidth semantics) would remove the guesswork agents rely on for layout tests.

pattern: canvas-rendered text invisible to DOM queries; DOM-presence assertions passed while the rendering was wrong
summary: To verify the new melt chart, the agent wrote UI checks that waited for axis labels via DOM selectors, but uPlot draws axes on canvas, so the waits timed out. A text-matched clickButton('Raw') hit the Raw view tab instead of the melt toggle. After the checks were rewritten to read DOM state, all 11 passed. A screenshot then showed the plot was still the amplification chart: a code edit had put the melt chart inside the rail, and the checks were reading that misplaced table. The agent fixed the placement and added a distinguishing class so the check could fail.
cost_estimate: ~7 min (03:16-03:23), ~20 tool calls: 4 scratch melt-only suite runs, 4 screenshots read as images, 2 patch scripts.
design_lesson: Canvas output has no queryable semantics. Chart and canvas APIs that expose an accessible or DOM-mirrored model (labels, series, axes) would let agents assert on what is drawn rather than on proxies.

api: Canvas / headless browser rendering vs hand-rolled rasterizer
pattern: reimplemented rendering and PNG encoding instead of using the browser's canvas
summary: Asked for a CLI PNG export matching the web chart, the agent chose a self-contained rasterizer to avoid deps and Chrome: png.mjs at 380 lines (a 5x7 font table, a PNG/CRC encoder, line/dash/circle coverage) plus about 350 lines of axis and tick layout. The user questioned the 728 new lines and suggested driving headless Chrome on the real chart. The agent agreed, bundled chart.ts and uPlot with esbuild into one HTML file (a file:// page can't load ES modules), screenshotted it via CDP, and deleted the rasterizer.
cost_estimate: 78 tool calls for the first implementation (02:02-02:20), then 53 to redo it (02:47-03:01), roughly 150k+ tokens. About an hour of wall-clock time including the discussion.
design_lesson: A cheap, documented way to render a page or component to an image headlessly (and to load a local module page without a server) would make 'use the browser' the obvious choice over reimplementing it.

pattern: closing the CDP WebSocket assumed to close the tab; ~25 tabs accumulated and slowed later tests
summary: The harness's cdp.close() closed only the WebSocket, so every test group left a live app tab behind. By group 23 about 25 tabs were competing for CPU, which made one group take 26s of setup. Profiling with timestamped output found it; closing the target saved ~25s of a 150s suite.
cost_estimate: Found within ~17 min of profiling; fix validated with 3 runs.
design_lesson: Contrast: a 'close' that releases only the connection and not the resource it names leaks silently.

api: Claude Code background shells / task notifications
pattern: orchestrator polls subagents with stacked background sleep shells instead of waiting for completion notifications
summary: While waiting for subagents, the orchestrator kept launching new background 'sleep 700-1200; git status' shells plus repeated ReadNotifications calls. Each completion prompted yet another shell, until 14 overlapped. The user asked whether that was right; the agent admitted the polling was unnecessary because subagent completion arrives as a notification anyway.
cost_estimate: Dozens of turns over hours. Each page of 100 events from 23:41 onward covers only about 1 minute of polling noise, at roughly 635k cached context per turn.
design_lesson: When completion is pushed, document clearly that it is pushed (no polling needed); otherwise agents default to polling.

pattern: document-level copy/paste listeners saw stale selection after click (React effect re-registration race)
summary: Window keydown/copy/paste listeners were re-registered in a React effect on every selection change. A scripted click followed by a copy event reached the old listener and copied the previous block. The new UI checks failed, and the agent first added waits in the tests and then moved the listener state into a ref so the listeners register once per edit mode. The root cause is framework state timing around global clipboard events, not Clipboard API semantics.
cost_estimate: ~12 min (14:32-14:44), 4 full UI-suite runs (~2.5 min each), ~10 tool calls.
design_lesson: Clipboard events go to the document rather than to an element-scoped editing context, which pushes apps into global listeners whose state can go stale; per-element copy/paste targets, or an async clipboard model tied to a focused element, would avoid this.

pattern: document-level copy/paste shortcuts swallowed when focus stays in a text input; synthetic clipboard events in tests hid it
summary: Cmd-C/Cmd-V did nothing in the plate editor. The handler skipped events while an input was focused (an 'inField' guard), and clicking a well did not move focus off the 'add a dye' or Sample field. The existing UI test synthesized clipboard events, so it never caught this. The agent wrote CDP probes with real keystrokes to see whether the events reached the window (they did, on BODY), then found focus stuck in an INPUT. The user had already diagnosed it. Fix: the grid takes focus on mousedown, and the test now uses the real gesture. Later the sweep test also needed a mouseover+mouseenter pair because React synthesizes onMouseEnter from mouseover.
cost_estimate: ~3 min and 2 throwaway CDP probe scripts (4 runs) to diagnose; a later test-iteration round for the React mouseover/mouseenter event pair (1 extra full UI run, ~80s).
design_lesson: Focus is invisible state that silently decides where keyboard and clipboard events go. Platform tooling that reports 'event X was routed to element Y because of focus' would remove this guesswork, and tests should use trusted input rather than synthetic events.

pattern: optional-chained click on a not-yet-rendered element silently no-ops; tests passed vacuously
summary: Test helpers like clickTab used `t?.click()` / `b && b.click()`. When the view bar hadn't rendered yet the click silently did nothing, and some checks then passed vacuously (one asserted on a Files tab that was never opened). Faster polling exposed this as flakes. The agent replaced the helpers with wait-for-element-then-click versions that fail loudly.
cost_estimate: ~10 min (14:32-14:44), 4 full UI runs.
design_lesson: Null-returning lookups combined with optional chaining hide failures; automation-oriented APIs (e.g. locator-style queries that wait and throw) make 'element not there' an explicit error.

pattern: read element textContent expecting it to include a child input's value
summary: The agent wrote a CDP/Puppeteer-style UI check that read the filename from the <dd> cell after Clone put the row into edit mode. textContent excludes form control values, so the check saw an empty string and timed out. A throwaway debug script showed the feature worked, and the assertion was changed to read input.value.
cost_estimate: ~4 tool calls (a debug script, 2 UI-suite runs of ~80s each), ~3 min wall clock
design_lesson: Form-control values living outside textContent is a classic DOM trap; an accessible-name/'visible text' accessor would match what agents expect.

pattern: delayed single-click by a timer to tell it apart from dblclick; synthetic dblclick skipped the click sequence
summary: To make a single click toggle a file without breaking double-click-to-open, the agent held each click for 250ms and cancelled it if a second click came, using MouseEvent.detail. It also noticed that its test dispatched a bare 'dblclick', which never runs the real click,click,dblclick sequence, and rewrote the test to dispatch all three. The user rejected the delay and asked for an immediate click with dblclick only navigating. That needed a second rework in which dblclick waits on the promise from the first click, because dblclick fires before React re-renders.
cost_estimate: 2 implementation rounds; ~40 min total (12:43-12:59, 13:16-13:25), ~5 full UI-suite runs.
design_lesson: Because the DOM always fires click before dblclick and gives no gesture-level 'this click will not become a double-click' signal, agents reach for timers; docs and test utilities should make the real event sequence explicit, and synthetic dblclick should not be the obvious way to simulate one.

pattern: element.blur() is a silent no-op on an element that was never focused
summary: To test an editable experiment-name field (committed on blur), the agent's CDP-evaluated test set the value via the HTMLInputElement value setter, dispatched 'input', then called el.blur(). The commit never happened. It first misdiagnosed this as React not having committed the draft in the same tick and split the steps (another full test run), then realised the field had never been focused so blur() fired nothing, and added focus() first.
cost_estimate: 2 wrong-then-right edit cycles, 3 browser-suite runs (~1 min each), ~3 min wall clock, ~10k tokens
design_lesson: Silent no-ops are agent traps: blur() on an unfocused element (and the React value-setter workaround needed to simulate typing) give no signal; a first-class 'simulate user edit' API or a console diagnostic for no-op focus calls would prevent misdiagnosis.

pattern: navigation implemented as <button> assigning location.hash instead of a real <a href>
summary: For 'Load an example file' the agent built a <button> whose handler assigned #load=... to location.hash, with a workaround because assigning an unchanged hash fires no hashchange. The user asked for it to be a link so the browser's 'Copy link address' works. The agent converted it to <a href="#load=..."> and kept preventDefault only for the same-hash case.
cost_estimate: follow-up task ~6 min, ~25 tool calls (plus a rebase onto a redesigned AboutView)
design_lesson: When navigation semantics live in a click handler rather than an href, the platform's link affordances silently disappear; the same-hash/no-hashchange quirk pushes agents toward script-driven navigation.

pattern: synthetic mouseover does not produce mouseenter/leave semantics
summary: The agent tested a hover-to-peek chip behaviour by dispatching synthetic "mouseover"/"mouseout" events. The assertion failed because React derives onMouseEnter/onMouseLeave from the over/out pair plus relatedTarget, which the synthetic events lacked. It switched to real CDP Input.dispatchMouseEvent pointer moves.
cost_estimate: One failed UI-suite run plus 3 tool calls, ~2 min.
design_lesson: dispatchEvent of one low-level event does not reproduce the event sequence the browser derives from it. A first-class "simulate pointer move to element" API (like WebDriver BiDi input) avoids the guess.

pattern: intermittent DOM-race test failure dismissed as flake after reruns
summary: While landing a feature, the full uitest failed with 'timed out waiting for runlog.xml to render'. The agent checked plain main, suspected its own per-render recomputation, then re-ran the suite 2 more times and declared it a flake ('passed 5 of 7 runs'). The real cause, a post-render useEffect race, was found and fixed in a separate session ~30 min later.
cost_estimate: ~5 min wall clock (20:40-20:45), 4 full UI-suite runs (~60 s each), ~12 tool calls
design_lesson: Without deterministic render-completion signals, agents spend reruns rather than diagnosis on timing-dependent UI failures.

pattern: hand-rolled follow-scroll fires on updates the user cannot see
summary: The user reported that the USB traffic console scrolled to the bottom even when nothing visible had been added, suspecting the follow and hide-polling options. The agent found the follow effect (scrollTop = scrollHeight) keyed on the filtered `lines` array, and changed the dependency to the raw `instrument.traffic`. My inference (not checked in-session): with hide-polling on, raw traffic changes on every hidden poll, so the effect still fires for invisible updates. That is arguably exactly the user's report, so the fix may be incomplete. Nothing was verified in a browser, only typechecked.
cost_estimate: About 3.5 minutes, 23 tool calls including 2 sub-agents. Cheap, but probably wrong; there was no browser verification.
design_lesson: The platform has no declarative 'stick to bottom while the user is at the bottom' scroll primitive (overflow-anchor doesn't cover it), so every log view hand-rolls scrollTop effects with subtle trigger bugs. A native follow-tail mode would remove the class of bug.

pattern: filtering at render time still triggers state updates and scroll effects, causing visible flicker
summary: The earlier 'hide polling' implementation filtered poll lines in the console's render. Each 1.5 s poll still updated React state, re-rendered the panel and re-ran its follow-scroll effect, and the user saw the console flash every poll. The agent moved the filter into the hook so suppressed lines never reach state. It is mostly a framework-level mistake; the visible symptom came from the DOM scroll effect.
cost_estimate: fix ~7 min (19:40-19:47), ~25 tool calls; the original bug cost a user report
design_lesson: Scroll-follow patterns (scrollTop = scrollHeight in an effect) are easy to re-trigger by accident; a native 'stick to bottom' scroll-anchoring primitive would remove the effect entirely.

api: File System Access (permission state, test emulation)
pattern: flaky 'folder permission has expired' UI checks require multiple full reruns
summary: After rebasing, the File System Access checks for an expired folder permission ('stays listed, with a read-error badge', 'clicking it retries') failed in 2 of 4 full UI runs. The agent checked that its check group left no state behind, then landed anyway. The same checks flaked in session_01VeMy and session_01LSsq.
cost_estimate: ~3 extra full UI runs (~85 s each), ~6 tool calls
design_lesson: Permission-state transitions (granted→prompt) that tests must simulate and wait on are hard to make deterministic; a testing hook to set permission state synchronously would help.

pattern: persisted directory handle permission lapses across reload; opaque NotAllowedError surfaced raw
summary: The app (built in earlier agent sessions) restored FileSystemDirectoryHandles from IndexedDB and read files on hydration without checking for lapsed permission, so the user saw Chrome's raw NotAllowedError text in a red error box and the file was dropped. The agent added isPermissionError (DOMException name NotAllowedError/SecurityError), kept the row with a read-error badge, and moved requestPermission to the click handler because it requires a user gesture.
cost_estimate: First turn ~18 min (11:44-12:02), ~150 tool calls incl. 3 full UI suite runs.
design_lesson: Permission-lapse failures should be a distinct, documented error (or a permission-state event) with an actionable message, and docs should state clearly that persisted handles need re-permission after reload.

pattern: assumed permission grants are per-handle; Chrome's restore prompt re-grants all handles at once
summary: After implementing click-to-regrant, the agent refreshed only the clicked file. The user had to ask for the folder's other files to reload, then correct again that Chrome re-grants every folder at once, so all folders should be rescanned. Each correction cost a new worktree, code change, new UI test, and repeated full browser-suite runs (some flaky under load).
cost_estimate: 2 extra user rounds, ~1h05m wall clock (12:27-13:32), ~370 events, ~10 full UI suite runs (~2.5 min each).
design_lesson: Permission scope (per handle vs. per origin) should be explicit in the API, e.g. a permission change event or a query over all granted handles, rather than discovered from browser UI behaviour.

pattern: assumed persisted FileSystemDirectoryHandle stays granted across reload; requestPermission needs user activation
summary: The agent made #file= links search granted disk folders. It treated a folder whose restored handle reported permission 'prompt', or whose read threw NotAllowedError, as 'not found' and silently gave up. The user reported 'It's not working'. The agent found the deploy lag, but also that a granted folder's permission almost always lapses to 'prompt' on reload, which is exactly when a link arrives, and that requestPermission can't be called without a gesture. Second commit: remember the awaiting folder, show a 'Grant access to that folder' prompt, and retry on grant.
cost_estimate: Second fix round ~10 min (03:22-03:32), ~45 tool calls, 2 full UI-suite runs plus 1 re-run for flakes; a second worktree and commit (+85/-5 UI, +47 UI tests).
design_lesson: Permission state for persisted handles should be observable and documented at the point of use, e.g. a typed 'needs-gesture' state or an event when a grant lapses, so 'prompt after reload' isn't learned by shipping a silent failure.

pattern: polling a file while the app holds an open writable stalled the page (lock contention)
summary: To replace a fixed 3.5s sleep, the agent polled the on-disk file's mtime every 100ms (via the OPFS-backed test folder) while the app was writing the same file. A later flake-hunt run hung in a 30s CDP Runtime.evaluate timeout. The agent attributed it to the exclusive lock an open FileSystemWritableFileStream holds and reverted to the sleep, adding a comment. The lock explanation was the agent's own diagnosis and was not verified further.
cost_estimate: 1 failed full UI run plus diagnosis (~17 min gap 15:01-15:18) and 1 verification run; the optimisation was worth ~0.5s.
design_lesson: File-handle locking semantics (which operations block behind an open writable, for how long, and whether they reject or wait) should be documented and observable; a read that silently queues is hard for an agent to diagnose.

api: File System Access API (showDirectoryPicker) under automation
pattern: permission picker can't be automated, so tests swap in OPFS
summary: The agent tried to drive showDirectoryPicker from headless Chrome via CDP Page.setInterceptFileChooserDialog. The intercept fires, but the call rejects with AbortError and there is no way to hand back a directory. For the UI tests it monkey-patched showDirectoryPicker to return an OPFS directory, and wrote an OPFS-rooted helper to simulate external writes. That helper had its own path bug ('walks from the OPFS root, so it needs the runs prefix').
cost_estimate: 1 probe and about 15 test-authoring/debug calls (02:52-03:01). The test fixture is a permanent extra layer.
design_lesson: Permission-gated pickers need a first-class WebDriver/CDP hook to supply a real directory, so agents can test the real code path instead of a stand-in.

pattern: no usable docs, so the agent probed API availability and semantics empirically
summary: Asked to build disk-backed folders with FSA and FileSystemObserver, the agent first searched the modern-web-guidance skill, which returned an empty result for FSA. It then wrote about 7 throwaway CDP probe scripts against headless Chrome 151 to find out which APIs exist and how they behave. The first two probes reported every API as undefined because the page wasn't a secure context (they ran on example.com, which reported secure:false). A localhost server fixed that. Later probes measured permission state, IndexedDB round-tripping of handles, FileSystemObserver record types and per-file watch behaviour.
cost_estimate: About 20 tool calls over 2 bursts (01:18-01:21 and 02:22-02:23), roughly 4 minutes of wall-clock time, about 15-25k tokens of probe scripts and output. Cheap compared with the 2.7h session, but every fact about the API came from probes, not from docs.
design_lesson: Machine-readable, agent-reachable docs and feature/permission introspection (including 'why is this undefined: insecure context') would replace probe scripts.

api: File System Access API typings (TypeScript lib.dom)
pattern: shipping APIs missing from TS lib.dom; hand-written ambient types
summary: The first typecheck of diskFolders.ts failed: 'FileSystemObserver' does not exist on globalThis, and 'entries' does not exist on FileSystemDirectoryHandle. The agent had already checked that TypeScript 5.9's lib.dom has OPFS-related FSA types but lacks showDirectoryPicker, queryPermission and FileSystemObserver. It wrote a fileSystemAccess.d.ts and added DOM.AsyncIterable to tsconfig so entries() resolves.
cost_estimate: About 4 tool calls and 1 failed typecheck, under 1 minute.
design_lesson: Agents often treat the type definitions as the API reference. When the typings lag shipped APIs, agents get pushed toward hand-rolled declarations that can drift.

pattern: observer silently stops after a watched file is deleted and recreated (atomic save)
summary: While designing per-file watches, the agent probed what happens on delete+recreate, which is what an external editor's atomic save looks like.
