The observer emits 'disappeared' then 'errored', and the observation is then dead: recreating the same path emits nothing. The app has to re-resolve the handle and call observe() again. Nothing in the API surface signals this; only a dedicated probe revealed it, and the agent added a regression test for the re-arm.
cost_estimate: 2 probe scripts (fsprobe6/7) plus a plan rewrite, about 1.5 minutes and roughly 8k tokens. It would have been a latent bug if not probed.
design_lesson: An observer that ends its own subscription should say so loudly (a terminal 'errored' with a reason, or auto-follow the path) and be documented, or every caller ships a silent-staleness bug.

pattern: flaky autofocus/focus assertion in headless Chrome forces a full UI-suite rerun
summary: The full browser suite failed 1 of 446 checks: the clone-a-run name field was 'required' but not focused. The agent saw it touched no changed code, reran the whole ~80 s suite, and it passed. The root cause of the focus flake was never investigated.
cost_estimate: 1 extra full UI run (~80 s), 2-3 tool calls
design_lesson: Focus outcomes in headless/background tabs depend on window focus state the page can't see; a deterministic focus model for automation (or a clear signal of why focus was refused) would remove the flake.

pattern: flaky autofocus/focus assertion in headless Chrome forces a full UI-suite rerun
summary: Same clone-flow 'focused for typing' check failed ({"focused":false}) on the second full UI run. A third full run passed and the agent called it a one-off focus flake.
cost_estimate: 1 extra full UI run (~80 s), 2 tool calls
design_lesson: Same as above: focus in automation needs to be deterministic or explain its refusal.

pattern: browser autofill heuristics offer unrelated saved data on bare numeric inputs
summary: Chrome offered a saved phone number on the protocol editor's bare <input type=number> fields (temperatures and hold times). The agent (likely prompted by mid-session user feedback; not visible in the user/assistant event stream) added autocomplete="off" with a comment explaining the heuristic.
cost_estimate: 1-2 tool calls
design_lesson: Opaque autofill heuristics are invisible to code-only agents; autofill defaults should not apply to unlabeled numeric inputs, or there should be a lint-visible signal.

pattern: intermittent hash-navigation race misread as environmental test flakiness
summary: The UI suite failed at 'cold deep link opens the named view' (it landed on Plates instead of Reference). The agent re-ran the suite with its change reverted, saw the same area fail, and called it pre-existing flakiness. This was the popstate/hashchange stale-write race that session_01Gyzu1yYVt8P3rnYUKiwLkL diagnosed and fixed six days later. It's recorded here for frequency.
cost_estimate: 2 extra full UI-suite runs (about 45 s each) plus a revert-and-retest of the file, about 4 tool calls.
design_lesson: Non-deterministic event ordering across two navigation events looks like environmental flakiness, so agents rationalize it away instead of fixing it.

pattern: popstate and hashchange are dispatched separately for one hash navigation; a render in between writes stale state back to the URL
summary: The app listens to both popstate and hashchange, because each alone misses some navigations, and has a passive React effect that writes state to the URL with pushState. On a hash navigation the effect could run between the two events and push the old view back over the new URL. The listener's second call (hashchange) then read the reverted URL, and deep links silently landed on the wrong tab, intermittently. The agent's first fix didn't help. It took a probe script that monkey-patched pushState/replaceState and logged popstate, hashchange and tab mutations, plus about 8 full UI-suite runs, before a sequence-counter fix worked.
cost_estimate: About 47 tool calls and 8 full UI-suite runs in about 10 minutes (22:32-22:42), plus about 4 minutes of triage before that. The episode is about 1.0M chars of raw transcript (roughly 100-250k tokens including tool output).
design_lesson: One navigation fires two events, in separate tasks, with no shared navigation id. A single 'URL changed' event with a navigation id, such as the Navigation API's navigate/currententrychange, would have made the race unwritable.

pattern: intermittent hash-navigation race misread as environmental test flakiness
summary: The full UI suite timed out at different checks on different runs ('timed out waiting for the well grid', 'protocol file's Overview', and others). The agent built a separate baseline worktree from main to show the failures were pre-existing, declared the timeouts environmental, and worked around them by running only the melt groups from a temporary copy of the suite. The well-grid timeout is the downstream symptom of the hash race fixed later in session_01Gyzu1yYVt8P3rnYUKiwLkL.
cost_estimate: About 5 full or baseline UI-suite runs and a baseline worktree setup, roughly 15 tool calls (02:38-03:06).
design_lesson: Same as the hash-race incident. An API that makes the race impossible saves the debugging and also the repeated misattribution across sessions.

pattern: IndexedDB unavailable on about:blank (opaque origin) gives a vague SecurityError
summary: To check the v1->v2 IndexedDB upgrade, the agent wrote a CDP script that seeded a v1 database. Its eval ran before the tab had navigated, so indexedDB.deleteDatabase threw 'access to the Indexed Database API is denied in this context' on about:blank. Earlier the IDB promise came back as {} because awaitPromise was missing, and the fixes also hit Page.navigate 'Invalid parameters' and an undefined origin, before the script navigated to the dev-server origin and passed.
cost_estimate: ~12 tool calls, ~2 min wall-clock (20:28:40-20:30:32), ~3-5k tokens
design_lesson: The SecurityError should name the cause (opaque origin / about:blank) and the fix; 'denied in this context' makes the agent probe its way to the answer.

pattern: stale belief about browser storage internals (IDB large-value compression)
summary: Asked whether storing ZIPs in IndexedDB is redundant compression, the agent confidently argued the opposite: Chrome's LevelDB Snappy-compresses blocks but 'large values are written to external files that bypass that path'. The user pointed it at Chrome's IndexedDB storage-improvements post; a WebFetch showed Chrome 129 compresses large external values too. The correction flipped the design to storing raw per-entry records and zipping only on download.
cost_estimate: ~20 min wall-clock (11:05-11:17 UTC 2026-08-05) across 3 AskUserQuestion rounds, 1 ToolSearch+WebFetch; the wrong premise shaped a 'measure first' harness proposal that was dropped; ~3-4k output tokens of discussion
design_lesson: Storage engines' performance traits (compression, size thresholds, partial-write cost) are undocumented and unobservable from the API; normative or queryable characteristics (or one canonical doc) would stop agents reasoning from outdated folklore.

pattern: no partial-record update forces whole-record rewrites; repeated schema redesigns
summary: IndexedDB can only put whole values, so each live-run plate read rewrote the whole ~965 KB archive record (and the size-hashed key even forced delete+put), ~45 MB of structured-clone traffic to append ~1 MB. Working around it took three schema redesigns over two days (exploded map-of-entries in 012WmWHN, meta/settings stores in 0173T67n, merged store + entry-per-record keyed [name, entry] with getAllKeys-based delta writes here), each needing rebases, UI test updates and ARCHITECTURE.md rewrites. The delta write then hit a write-ordering race the agent had to debug from flaky tests.
cost_estimate: This session alone: 787 events, ~46k output tokens, ~74.6M cache-read tokens, ~1h45m of active work (10:32-12:27); plus sessions 012WmWHN (~46k out) and 0173T67n (~25k out) on earlier storage shapes
design_lesson: A storage API with no partial update or append primitive pushes every app to hand-roll a chunked key schema and diffing; an append/patch operation, or documented guidance on record granularity, would avoid repeated redesigns.

pattern: persisted IndexedDB state leaks between test cases sharing one browser profile
summary: In the UI suite, a CFX run left open in IndexedDB re-hydrated in the next page, so a wait matched the wrong file's melt toggle (a '2 vs 0' flake). Later the Biomeme melt run left in the database made the next check count 27 rows from the wrong file. Each needed diagnosis and an explicit indexedDB.deleteDatabase or emptyReload.
cost_estimate: 2 diagnoses, ~3 extra suite runs (~1-2 min each).
design_lesson: Origin storage that persists across navigations needs cheap, awaitable isolation primitives for tests (per-test storage partitions or reset), not hand-written deleteDatabase dances.

api: IndexedDB (origin-persistent storage in a shared test profile)
pattern: persistent IndexedDB state leaks between test pages; misdiagnosed as pre-existing flake
summary: A UI check the agent had added the day before loaded a .pcrd and left the run in IndexedDB. Every later page in the same Chrome profile rehydrated and re-analysed it, which pushed the Cq-filter checks past their fixed 200 ms sleeps about one run in three. The agent stashed its changes and reran 'pristine' HEAD, but the profile still held the leaked run, so it told the user the failure was 'pre-existing flakiness'. Disabling its new check finally isolated the cause. The fix deletes the run afterwards and waits for the expected effect instead of sleeping.
cost_estimate: About 37 tool calls over 03:45-03:59 (about 14 min), with many full UI-suite runs of about 30 s each. About 47k chars of transcript (roughly 12k tokens).
design_lesson: Storage that silently outlives a page makes test state invisible. An easy way to list or reset an origin's storage (or per-test storage partitions) would have made the leak obvious, and so would events that signal 'app idle' so tests don't need fixed sleeps.

api: IndexedDB (origin-persistent storage in a shared test profile)
pattern: persistent IndexedDB state leaks between test pages; misdiagnosed as pre-existing flake
summary: A parallel session hit the same UI-test failures (5 Cq-range checks). It reran the suite with and without its change and stashed and unstashed. It concluded 'pre-existing flake' and landed anyway, without finding the cause: the IndexedDB leak from another session's test (see 0199FR). This is a second occurrence of the same failure mode.
cost_estimate: About 8 tool calls over 03:59-04:08 (about 9 min), mostly 30-60 s full UI-suite runs.
design_lesson: Same as above: invisible persistent storage across test pages, plus fixed sleeps, produce flakes that agents misattribute.

pattern: fixed sleeps and silently-expiring waits standing in for unobservable async browser state
summary: The user asked why tests were slow. The agent found agent-written UI tests waiting for changes that could never happen: two resetWells() waits hit an 8s timeout each, and a folder check burned 10s behind .catch(()=>{}), all still passing. Many sleeps stood in for browser state with no obvious signal: an IndexedDB delete transaction committing, a Page.navigate to about:blank settling, write-behind flushes, and uPlot painting on rAF. The agent replaced them with waits on real observables (reading the IndexedDB catalog, polling location.href) and made every soft timeout fail the run, which surfaced two more real flakes.
cost_estimate: Two sessions' worth: ~15 min (21:27-21:41) and ~30 min (01:24-01:54), ~12 full UI-suite runs; the suite went from 97s to ~55s.
design_lesson: Async platform operations (IndexedDB commit, navigation and context swap, first paint) need awaitable completion signals that test tooling can hook. Without them agents fall back to sleeps that hide bugs and burn time.

pattern: persisted IndexedDB state hydrating asynchronously races test setup
summary: A new UI check (the standalone .pltd XML tab renders as a tree) flaked intermittently. First the agent replaced sleeps with state waits. Then it found that the Chrome profile still held runs from earlier pages in IndexedDB, so the app sometimes hydrated a different file as active. Last, loadFile looked for the file input before the app re-rendered after a reload. The fixes were an emptyReload helper that clears IndexedDB, and a wait inside loadFile in the shared harness.
cost_estimate: 12:53-13:05, ~12 min and ~10 tool calls that ran the ~16s UI suite about 20 times in total.
design_lesson: Apps that restore state asynchronously from storage have no standard "ready/hydrated" signal, and storage is shared across pages in a profile. A per-context storage-isolation primitive plus an observable app-readiness hook would make such races obvious.

pattern: no observable completion for a write-behind IndexedDB flush; reload aborts the in-flight write, so tests used fixed sleeps
summary: The test harness forces the app's throttled writes to flush by dispatching visibilitychange to hidden, then reloads. flushWrites starts the IndexedDB flush without awaiting it, so the reload aborted the write and a persistence check failed on almost every run. The agent fixed that test by polling the stored IndexedDB record until it held the edit. The user then asked it to remove the other uses of fixed waits, and six post-flush sleeps were each replaced with waits on the actual stored record.
cost_estimate: About 6 tool calls for the first fix (22:44-22:46), then about 15 more tool calls and 2 full suite runs to replace six sleeps (23:01-23:05).
design_lesson: A page has no way to tell outsiders 'my storage writes are durable now', and an unload silently aborts pending IndexedDB transactions. An awaitable flush/durability signal, or a reliable 'complete before unload' guarantee, would replace sleep-based waiting.

pattern: drag state ended only on mouseup; contextmenu swallows mouseup so a right-click mid-drag leaves the drag armed
summary: The plate editor's drag-select (written by an earlier agent session) started on any mousedown and ended only on a window mouseup. A right-click opens the context menu, which swallows the mouseup, so after the menu closed the next mouse move kept extending the selection. The user reported 'right-click doesn't cancel a drag-select'. Fix: ignore non-primary buttons (e.button===0), end the drag on contextmenu, and add a TODO to move the whole app to Pointer Events, because pointercancel is the platform's 'gesture over' signal.
cost_estimate: Small fix (~6 edits) inside a 53-min, five-bug session; plus a new negative UI check (sleep-based by repo rule).
design_lesson: A gesture API should guarantee a terminal event (pointerup/pointercancel), and docs and examples should steer away from mousedown/mouseup pairs whose end can be silently eaten.

api: Mouse/pointer events (drag over a canvas chart)
pattern: drag built from window mouse listeners without capture; underlying chart's hover still tracks the pointer
summary: For drag-to-adjust on Cq markers, the agent used mousedown on the chart host plus window mousemove/mouseup, with no pointer events or setPointerCapture. Its headless test checked ring position and passed 12/12. The user then reported flicker: uPlot's own cursor, tooltip and hover points kept reacting to the same mouse moves, re-created on every rebuilt frame. The fix was pointer-events:none on uPlot's overlay during the drag plus tooltip suppression.
cost_estimate: About 15 tool calls and 9 minutes for the follow-up fix, roughly 20k tokens. It also needed a separate user round-trip after the feature had landed.
design_lesson: Gestures need an obvious exclusive-ownership primitive (pointer capture that also suppresses hover on other targets); otherwise agents reach for window mousemove and miss the side effects their headless tests can't see.

pattern: expected fragment-only navigation to reload the page
summary: A rewritten UI test navigated to the same URL with a different #file= fragment and expected the app to re-hydrate from scratch. A fragment-only change is a same-document navigation, so no reload happened and the check failed. The agent noticed after a full browser-suite run and routed the navigation via about:blank to force a real load.
cost_estimate: 1 extra full UI-suite run (~2.5 min) plus one edit; ~3k tokens.
design_lesson: Navigation APIs could make same-document versus cross-document behaviour explicit in their signature or result, e.g. a 'reload' option or a returned navigation type.

pattern: relative import path from a scratch dir outside the repo
summary: The agent wrote a scratch script in ~/.claude/jobs/<id>/tmp that imported the harness via a relative "../../../code/zpcrweb/..." path. Node resolved it from the script location, giving ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND, and the agent switched to an absolute path.
cost_estimate: 1-2 tool calls, <1 min
design_lesson: Contrast case: module specifiers resolve relative to the importing file, which agents lose track of when writing scripts in temp directories.

pattern: relative import path from a scratch dir outside the repo
summary: The agent wrote a scratch script in ~/.claude/jobs/<id>/tmp that imported the harness via a relative "../../../code/zpcrweb/..." path. Node resolved it from the script location, giving ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND, and the agent switched to an absolute path.
cost_estimate: 1-2 tool calls, <1 min
design_lesson: Contrast case: module specifiers resolve relative to the importing file, which agents lose track of when writing scripts in temp directories.

pattern: relative import path from a scratch dir outside the repo
summary: The agent wrote a scratch script in ~/.claude/jobs/<id>/tmp that imported the harness via a relative "../../../code/zpcrweb/..." path. Node resolved it from the script location, giving ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND, and the agent switched to an absolute path.
cost_estimate: 1-2 tool calls, <1 min
design_lesson: Contrast case: module specifiers resolve relative to the importing file, which agents lose track of when writing scripts in temp directories.

pattern: agent reaches for a bundler-runner to import app-layer code instead of a library boundary
summary: Asked for a simple CLI, the agent wrote tools/zpcr.ts, which ran under vite-node and imported analysis logic from apps/web/src. The user asked whether it depended on UI code and why it needed vite. The agent confirmed real dependency and duplication, then moved six modules into packages/core so the CLI became a thin plain-node script. The UI and CLI then shared identical CSV code.
cost_estimate: ~12:03–12:35 (~30 min) refactor round, ~150 tool calls
design_lesson: (Contrast) Agents follow the path of least resistance across module boundaries; APIs and packages that make the 'right' import the easy one prevent this.

pattern: test harness imported stale built dist; checks silently skipped
summary: The UI test harness imported packages/core/dist, which was older than the source, and the app under test used source through a Vite alias. A missing export aborted the suite partway, leaving about 44 of 211 checks unexercised. The agent ruled out importing source directly (Node type-stripping doesn't resolve .js specifiers) and added a buildCore() step.
cost_estimate: ~15 tool calls, ~4 min
design_lesson: n/a (tooling).

pattern: no supported way to drive document.visibilityState in automation; CDP method removed, freeze never thaws
summary: The user suggested tests hide and show the page to force the app's visibilitychange flush instead of waiting out a 3s write timer. The agent's first probe failed because Emulation.setPageVisibilityState no longer exists in Chrome. Page.setWebLifecycleState('frozen') fired a real visibilitychange but the page never returned to visible. The final helper monkeypatches document.visibilityState with Object.defineProperty and dispatches a synthetic visibilitychange.
cost_estimate: 4 throwaway probe scripts, ~5 min (17:02-17:06), ~12 tool calls, ~8k tokens.
design_lesson: Lifecycle states that apps are told to handle (hidden, frozen, bfcache) need a stable, standard automation hook (e.g. WebDriver BiDi) so agents can test them without monkeypatching document properties.

api: Page Visibility API / CDP lifecycle emulation
pattern: no supported way to make a page 'hidden' from automation; removed CDP method and a lifecycle freeze that never thaws
summary: To make tests flush the app's rate-limited IndexedDB and disk writes without sleeping, the agent wanted to fire visibilitychange to hidden, which production already uses as its flush trigger. Chrome had removed Emulation.setPageVisibilityState. Page.setWebLifecycleState froze the page and didn't reliably thaw it, leaving it hidden with every timer throttled afterwards. The agent settled on overriding document.visibilityState just long enough to dispatch the event. The flush was also fire-and-forget (void flushAll()), so callers still had to poll storage; that later caused the reload-aborts-write flake fixed in session_01Gyzu1yYVt8P3rnYUKiwLkL. The agent also found that several checks had only passed by accident because navigation fired pagehide.
cost_estimate: Unknown. The trial-and-error happened in the part of the transcript I couldn't read; only the agent's summary of the outcome is visible.
design_lesson: Lifecycle states (hidden, frozen, discarded) can't be reliably driven or awaited by tools, and lifecycle-triggered work has no completion signal. A supported test or WebDriver BiDi hook to set visibility, plus awaitable lifecycle work, would replace hacks and sleeps.

api: Popover API (hidePopover / light dismiss / top layer)
pattern: programmatic popover dismissal races mount/unmount; hidePopover throws on non-popover; synthetic Escape doesn't reach top layer
summary: The UI test closed the step-form popover by calling hidePopover(). That threw 'NotSupportedError: ... Not supported on elements that are not popovers' once React had torn the element down. The agent switched to a synthesized Escape keypress, which never reached the popover, and then to a pointer light-dismiss, which missed when the popover flipped above its row. Instrumented runs finally showed the real cause: closeForm ran in the frame before the effect that calls showPopover, so hiding did nothing. The fix was to wait for :popover-open, then call a guarded hidePopover().
cost_estimate: ~19:02–19:20 (~18 min wall clock), ~7 full UI-suite runs (~80s each) plus a standalone debug script, ~25 tool calls; 3 wrong hypotheses before the right one
design_lesson: Popover state changes are silent no-ops or throw depending on timing; an awaitable open/close (promise or 'toggle' guarantees) and a hidePopover that is idempotent on detached/non-popover elements would remove the guesswork.

pattern: effect runs late and compares lagging prop to moved-on ref, resetting state
summary: The undo/redo history hook reset itself after edits, so Undo stayed disabled in the UI test. The agent first rewrote the hook to avoid stale closures, which didn't fix it. It then checked Unicode code points of the button glyphs, injected window.__log instrumentation into the component, and temporarily disabled all other UI-test sections. The log showed Preact running a queued effect late against a lagging prop, and the guard was changed to recognise any text the hook itself had produced.
cost_estimate: 17:00–17:16 (~16 min), ~20 tool calls incl. 6 UI-suite runs (~80s each), 2 probe scripts, temporary instrumentation
design_lesson: Framework-level effect timing is invisible from code; observable state-transition logs (or devtools-style traces exposed to agents) shortcut this kind of hunt.

pattern: effect cleanup disposes a long-lived object; StrictMode replays the cleanup and latches it closed
summary: An earlier agent moved the USB session into a core CfxSession, and the React hook's effect cleanup disposed it. StrictMode's dev-mode mount/unmount/mount replays that cleanup, so the session latched closed and auto-reconnect after a dropped USB pipe was dead in every dev build. A reviewer subagent found it during the branch review, and connect() now reopens a disposed session.
cost_estimate: Found in review; verifying it took about 1 tool call. The fix was part of a larger commit.
design_lesson: Lifecycle APIs that intentionally double-invoke cleanup need idempotent dispose/reopen semantics, or the framework should warn when a disposed resource is reused.

api: React internals (fiber tree via DOM container)
pattern: walked a stale alternate React root fiber from the DOM node in a DevTools snippet
summary: The user asked for a DevTools snippet to download the in-memory binary USB log. The session object lives in a React ref, so the agent walked the fiber tree from the root DOM node's internal key. That fiber was the stale alternate copy with no children, and the snippet threw 'CfxSession not found'. The agent switched to the FiberRoot's .current. The user then asked for the real fix in code instead.
cost_estimate: 2 user round-trips, ~4 tool calls, ~3 min
design_lesson: No supported way to reach app state from DevTools pushes agents into private framework internals; contrast case for explicit, documented debug hooks.

pattern: unstable prop identity (`[]` literal) rebuilds a canvas chart each render, wiping hover state
summary: Making hover stateful caused a re-render on every mousemove. An unrelated prop, darkCurves={[]}, had a new identity on every render, so the uPlot chart was torn down and rebuilt each time and its tooltip and cursor were lost. The agent wrote a CDP probe script that dispatched mouse moves and logged mousemove counts, elementFromPoint, tooltip and cursor state. Comparing against a stashed baseline isolated the cause.
cost_estimate: About 20 tool calls, including 3 rewrites of a debug script, about 6 minutes (12:10-12:16).
design_lesson: Imperative canvas widgets wrapped in declarative frameworks lose state silently when they're recreated. A warning when a heavy widget is rebuilt each render would surface this.

api: React useEffect / DOM render timing (CDP UI test)
pattern: post-render effect resets state, leaving a frame rendered in stale mode that a DOM-polling test observes
summary: A uitest ('runlog.xml renders as the XML tree') flaked. RawFilesView reset the decode mode in a post-render useEffect, so the newly selected file first rendered in the previous file's mode. The test clicked a mode button during that frame. The agent reproduced it in an isolated 20x loop, failing on iteration 2, and confirmed the mechanism by dumping the filename and mode. It fixed it by resetting during render and anchoring the test on the filename, then confirmed the app fix was load-bearing by reverting it.
cost_estimate: ~10 min (21:16-21:26), ~40 tool calls. Plus ~5 min of 3 dismissed reruns in session_012Xvqkeo1aERahZTmC2BQFg the same day
design_lesson: UI test harnesses need a 'settled render' signal; polling DOM for a state that is transiently wrong makes flakes cheap to create and expensive to diagnose.

pattern: observer attaches to a null ref once and silently never observes; regression from 'harmless' dependency removal
summary: The user reported the header no longer collapsed to icons when it didn't fit. An earlier agent commit had dropped activeId from useHeaderFit's deps, reasoning that tab labels no longer change per file. But that dep was the only thing that re-ran the effect when .app__header went from not rendered (welcome screen) to rendered. ref.current stayed null, ResizeObserver never attached, and fit stayed at 0 with no error. It took about 9 minutes of debug scripts and console-capture instrumentation to find; the fix was a callback ref so the effect re-runs whenever the DOM node changes.
cost_estimate: 15:09–15:19 (~10 min) to root cause and fix, ~35 tool calls incl. debug scripts, a worktree rebase and console capture; plus the earlier regression commit itself
design_lesson: Observer APIs that need an element at subscribe time fail silently when there isn't one yet; element-lifecycle-aware observation (observe a selector/root, or warn on observing nothing) would make this robust and debuggable.

pattern: no text layout/collision avoidance in SVG; label placement fixed by render-screenshot-adjust loops
summary: For a markdown report the agent generated static SVG charts in a Node script. It then needed several headless-Chrome screenshot cycles to fix overlapping labels and spacing, because SVG text has no measurement or collision avoidance. The final cycles moved per-panel label offsets by hand.
cost_estimate: ~4 render/screenshot/Read-image cycles, ~15 tool calls, ~10 min
design_lesson: Static SVG gives an agent no way to measure or auto-place text without rendering, so only visual feedback reveals collisions; layout-aware text primitives would cut the loop.

pattern: assumed navigating to a URL that differs only in #fragment reloads the page
summary: The new GitHub check navigated the test page (CDP Page.navigate) to a URL whose fragment carried #github=... and expected the app to boot with it. Only the fragment changed, so it was a same-document navigation. The page never reloaded, the startup-only #github= handling never ran, and the check timed out. The agent wrote a debug script that dumped the app state (repos: null, hash: #view=curves), realized the cause, and went through about:blank first (the harness's existing navigateBlank helper) to force a real load.
cost_estimate: About 8 tool calls, including a custom debug script, about 2 minutes (17:55-17:57).
design_lesson: Whether a navigation is same-document or a full load depends silently on the URL diff. An explicit API, or a navigation result that says which kind happened, would make it obvious.

pattern: per-packet decoding without reassembly misreads continuation bytes of multi-packet bulk transfers as new messages
summary: While cross-checking usb.md against real captures, the agent found the repo's Python pcap decoder treated each USB bulk packet independently. Continuation bytes of large file transfers were misread as fresh channel-0/3 messages, which had produced a false 'channel 0 carries big garbled blobs' claim in the doc. The agent wrote an independent stateful reassembler, fixed the tool, and diffed the two until they agreed.
cost_estimate: ~32 tool calls over ~14 min (02:39-02:53) before the doc rewrite started
design_lesson: Transport APIs that deliver whole logical messages rather than raw packets (and say so in their docs) stop every consumer from re-deriving framing and reassembly.

pattern: API missing from TypeScript DOM lib (Chromium-only API)
summary: Asked to detect Chromium via navigator.userAgentData.brands, the agent first wrote typed access, then found that lib.dom.d.ts has no NavigatorUAData and fell back to an `as unknown as` cast. To test the non-Chromium path it overrode navigator.userAgentData via CDP addScriptToEvaluateOnNewDocument, since no other browser was available.
cost_estimate: ~5 tool calls, ~30 s; small
design_lesson: Single-engine APIs that aren't in shared type definitions push agents to untyped casts, which removes the main guardrail agents rely on.

pattern: config change committed but running server not restarted
summary: The user asked to expose the dev server on the LAN and restart it. The agent set server.host:true and committed, but didn't merge or restart the running Vite process (bound to [::1]) until the user had reported 'connection timed out' twice. It then killed and restarted it and confirmed *:5173.
cost_estimate: ~15 min wall clock of user waiting; small token cost
design_lesson: Contrast case: process lifecycle, not web API.

pattern: agent cannot test non-Chromium browsers; side effect on user's desktop
summary: Asked whether it could run UI tests on Safari or Firefox, the agent found its account had no GUI session, Apple Events were blocked, there was no geckodriver or Playwright, and the harness was CDP-only. Its probe `open -a Safari` launched Safari on the real user's desktop, which it then quit. Conclusion: only headless Chrome is testable, so cross-browser claims rest on the human.
cost_estimate: ~6 tool calls, ~1 min
design_lesson: A standard headless, cross-engine automation path (WebDriver BiDi everywhere, headless Safari) is a precondition for agents to verify interop at all.

pattern: unverified assumption about what an opaque transferIn NetworkError means
summary: The user reported "Failed to execute 'transferIn' on 'USBDevice': A transfer error has occurred", after which the device dropped. Without consulting the spec or docs, the agent asserted that Chrome throws this "for a stalled or babbling endpoint" and that the endpoint "is usually readable again on the very next call". It wrapped transferIn in 4 retries 200ms apart, treating usb.opened===false as the real-unplug signal. In WebUSB a stall is reported as result.status==='stall' (recovered with clearHalt), not thrown. The retry code never inspected status or called clearHalt, so the fix rests on guessed semantics and its unit tests only mock a thrown Error. Whether it helped on hardware was not confirmed in the session.
cost_estimate: About 9 minutes of wall clock (19:49–19:58), roughly 60 main-thread tool calls plus 3 Explore sub-agents. About 40K chars (~10K tokens) of condensed transcript. No doc lookups at all; the cost is mostly in confidently encoding a guess.
design_lesson: A single generic NetworkError message for every transferIn failure invites guessing. Distinct, documented failure kinds (stall vs babble vs disconnect vs timeout), or a result.status that covers them, would let an agent pick the right recovery (clearHalt, retry, or reconnect) instead of retrying blindly.

pattern: CDP-synthesized input grants user activation, so requestDevice() opens a chooser and hangs instead of rejecting
summary: To reproduce a bug headless, the agent typed a run name via CDP, then clicked 'Connect over USB' expecting requestDevice() to reject (no gesture, so the 'Fake device' fallback appears). The typing had given the page transient user activation, so requestDevice() opened a device chooser that headless Chrome never resolves and the rail sat on 'Connecting…'. The agent first guessed a blocking confirm() dialog, tried Page.handleJavaScriptDialog (none open), then read the connect path. It fixed the repro by sleeping 6 s so the activation lapsed.
cost_estimate: ~6 tool calls and 4 headless repro runs, ~3 min wall clock (00:00:28→00:03:40), roughly 15-20K tokens of transcript
design_lesson: requestDevice()'s outcome depends on invisible, time-limited user-activation state, and a chooser that cannot be shown (headless) hangs forever rather than rejecting; an explicit activation query plus a guaranteed rejection when no chooser can be shown would make it hard to misuse.

pattern: exclusive claimInterface held by browser tab blocks agent's out-of-band probe
summary: To probe the instrument directly, the agent ran its node-usb WebUSB-shim CLI. claimInterface failed with an opaque OS error (0xe00002c5) because the user's browser tab already had the interface claimed. The agent correctly inferred the cause, stopped, and asked the user to press Disconnect, then probed. No wrong turn, but the agent needed a human round-trip, and the error text never says who owns the device.
cost_estimate: ~4 tool calls plus one human round-trip (~4 min idle waiting for user); small token cost
design_lesson: Exclusive-resource errors should say who holds the resource and how to release it (e.g. 'claimed by another origin/process'), so an agent can act without guessing from a platform error code.

pattern: assumed USBDevice.open() starts with an empty IN pipe; stale replies from the previous connection are read first
summary: The CFX client sends one command at a time and pairs each channel-1 reply with the oldest pending request. After a page reload or Disconnect/Connect, a STATUS? reply the instrument had written for the previous connection was still queued on the bulk IN endpoint. The first transferIn returned it as the answer to *IDN?, and every later reply was off by one. The user found it from a screenshot of the Identity panel showing a status line as the model and a file listing as the firmware. The fix makes identify() reject replies that don't look like an identity until the real one arrives, and the emulator now keeps unread replies across close.
cost_estimate: 23 tool calls, ~8 min wall clock (01:44:31→01:52:14), roughly 30K tokens; landed as eda3155
design_lesson: WebUSB gives no way to flush or drain an endpoint on open and documents nothing about data surviving close/open, so agents assume a fresh pipe; a documented 'stale data may be pending' caveat or a drain primitive would prevent this.

pattern: permission-gated device chooser (requestDevice) cannot be automated, so a fake navigator.usb is needed to test connected UI
summary: After building the Device view, the agent could see only the disconnected state, because WebUSB permission can't be granted to headless Chrome (requestDevice needs a user gesture and a chooser). It wrote a mock-device unit test for the read pump/queue, then a one-off CDP script that installs a fake `navigator.usb` replaying the real instrument's recorded responses, just to screenshot the connected UI. It worked, but the agent had to hand-build a device simulator because the platform has no automation hook.
cost_estimate: ~2.5 min, ~10 tool calls, two new test artifacts (mock test file plus ~100-line fake-WebUSB script), roughly 15-20k tokens
design_lesson: Permissioned device APIs need a standard automation surface (a WebDriver/BiDi command to pre-grant a device or inject a virtual USB device, as WebBluetooth's simulated-adapter work does) so agents can test real flows without writing bespoke fakes.

pattern: transferIn failures retried uniformly; error kind only distinguishable by message regex
summary: The existing read pump (written in earlier sessions) retried every transferIn rejection 4x on the same handle, built for Chrome's 'NetworkError: A transfer error has occurred' (stall). The user regularly hit 'transferIn error: Cancelled', which no retry can fix, and the connection died. The agent reasoned that Cancelled / NotFoundError / InvalidStateError mean the handle is gone, made them fatal, added clearHalt before stall retries and a reconnect loop using getDevices() and the navigator.usb 'connect' event. Classification ended up as a regex over err.name+err.message because Chrome reuses NetworkError for both stalls and unplugs and 'Cancelled' has no distinct name.
cost_estimate: ~250 events; analysis turn + ~60 tool calls for implementation/tests; ~30 min wall clock (12:52-13:06 impl). No trial-and-error, but the root bug recurred for the user over multiple days.
design_lesson: WebUSB transfer errors should carry distinct, documented, machine-readable reasons (stall vs. cancelled vs. disconnected) and say whether the handle is still usable, instead of overloading NetworkError and relying on message text.

pattern: claimInterface fails because another context holds the device; opaque OS error code
summary: Running its Node CLI against the instrument, the agent hit 'claimInterface error: could not open interface for exclusive access (error 0xe00002c5)' twice. It guessed correctly that the user's browser tab held the device and waited until the user said 'try again now'. Later, during a live run, the read pump died with 'transferIn: Cancelled'. The agent never root-caused that error and worked around it by opening a fresh connection per poll.
cost_estimate: About 6 tool calls plus a user round-trip (03:06-03:13, about 7 minutes of waiting), and a workaround script per poll.
design_lesson: Exclusive-access failures should name the holder (or at least say 'claimed by another context'), and transfer cancellations should say why, instead of leaving agents to guess from raw OS error codes.

pattern: app-level USB 'traffic log' silently lossy: retried transferIn errors and transferOut failures not recorded; raw bytes dropped for text-like payloads
summary: The agent built a 'complete' USB traffic log for reverse-engineering, using its own new formatTrafficLog. The user asked how complete it really was, and the agent audited it. Text-classified messages kept only the decoded string, not the hex. transferIn retries (up to 4) that eventually succeeded left no log entry beyond a console.error, and transferOut failures weren't reported at all. Nothing below reassembled messages, such as per-packet framing or endpoint and stall details, was captured. The agent added an onTransferError callback on CfxDevice, always-hex log lines, UI rendering of errors and retries, and tests.
cost_estimate: 12:15–12:27 (~12 min) follow-up round, ~45 tool calls incl. core tests
design_lesson: WebUSB has no built-in traffic tap or transfer-error event stream, so every app hand-rolls a lossy log; a devtools-style or event-based capture of transfers (with status and retries) would give agents ground truth for reverse-engineering.

pattern: asserted on text that is painted into a canvas
summary: To verify a new Column x-axis mode, the agent queried ".u-label" text for the axis label. uPlot paints axis labels into the canvas, so the DOM query returned empty and the check failed. It switched to asserting on series counts and noted the limitation in a comment.
cost_estimate: One failed UI run plus 2 tool calls, ~1.5 min.
design_lesson: Canvas content is invisible to DOM queries and to the accessibility tree. A canvas-drawn chart that exposes its text semantically would let agents (and AT) verify it directly.

pattern: tool path sandbox rejects screenshot filePath repeatedly
summary: take_screenshot with a filePath failed three times with 'not within any of the configured workspace roots', using the jobs tmp dir, a relative path and the absolute repo path. It worked only once filePath was omitted.
cost_estimate: 4 tool calls, about 20 s.
design_lesson: Errors should say which roots are allowed (or what the default does), so the caller can fix the call on the first retry.

pattern: tool reports success for a file path that doesn't exist
summary: To load a sample into the page, the agent used chrome-devtools upload_file. A relative path was refused as outside workspace roots. An absolute path to a nonexistent file returned 'File uploaded from …', and the agent noticed only because the next snapshot showed nothing loaded. It ran ls and find to locate the real samples/ directory and uploaded again.
cost_estimate: ~5 tool calls, <1 min
design_lesson: File-input automation (and setInputFiles-style APIs) should fail loudly when the file doesn't exist instead of reporting success.

api: fetch / static file serving (dev-server SPA fallback)
pattern: missing static file returns 200 text/html SPA fallback, so a fetch-based load fails silently
summary: To check the new baseline ticks visually, the agent opened the app at #load=examples/20260720_FirstQualification.zpcr through chrome-devtools. The page silently stayed on the welcome screen. curl showed the Vite dev server answering the missing file with HTTP 200, Content-Type text/html, 704 bytes (the index.html fallback), so a fetch().ok check passes. Seven more calls (ls, readlink, stat, git ls-files) showed that only one sample was symlinked into public/examples.
cost_estimate: About 10 tool calls over 23:41:58-23:42:54 (about 1 min). About 8k chars of transcript.
design_lesson: A 200 response with an HTML body for a missing binary resource defeats response.ok. Apps and agents should check Content-Type, and dev servers should not fall back to the SPA page for paths with file extensions.

pattern: resolved CSS variables once via getComputedStyle into SVG attributes, so the theme didn't follow toggles
summary: For a dashboard artifact the agent wrote a helper `cv = n => getComputedStyle(document.documentElement).getPropertyValue(n)` and baked the resolved colours into SVG fill attributes. That freezes whichever theme was active at load. It caught this when inspecting a dark-mode screenshot, and switched to live `var(--x)` references. The first rewrite missed dynamic cv(c.v) calls, which an assertion caught.
cost_estimate: ~1.5 min, 4 tool calls plus 2 renders.
design_lesson: getComputedStyle returns a snapshot with no hint that it goes stale. Docs and lint for 'resolved vs live' values, or SVG presentation attributes that accept var(), would steer agents to the live form.

pattern: concurrent agent reset shared branch, silently discarding other agents' fast-forwarded commits
summary: The agent fast-forwarded its docs commit onto local main, but the user later found it missing. Reflog forensics showed another parallel agent had run 'git reset' to move main to its redone branch, which discarded this commit and one other (an 11-file feature). The agent recovered both via cherry-pick, re-ran the full suites, tested the user's 'git fetch . HEAD:main' idea in a throwaway repo, and proposed AGENTS.md wording.
cost_estimate: ~2h45m wall clock across follow-ups (18:17-20:43), ~450 events, 1 full UI-suite run.
design_lesson: Contrast: a destructive primitive (reset) available alongside a safe one (ff-only) lets one agent silently undo another's work; making the safe path the only easy path is the analogous API lesson.

pattern: agent force-moved shared main with reset --hard to land a rewritten commit, discarding others' work
summary: After the user asked for a simpler implementation, the agent soft-reset and squashed its already-landed commit into a new one. It then ran `git reset --hard worktree-plate-channel-lines-2` on the shared main checkout instead of rebasing. Two commits that other parallel agents had fast-forwarded onto main in the meantime vanished without warning; the loss was only found later, in another session, by the user.
cost_estimate: The reset itself was one command; the recovery cost about 2h of another session (see session_01TwEFG68JTJjnmPNKokj32U).
design_lesson: Contrast: when the destructive operation is as easy to reach as the safe one, an agent under a 'land it' goal takes it; safe-by-default primitives (ff-only, compare-and-swap ref updates) prevent silent loss.

pattern: literal NUL byte in source made git treat a file as binary
summary: During a rebase, db.ts showed no conflict markers. The cause was an earlier agent session writing the IndexedDB WHOLE_FILE sentinel as a literal NUL byte in a string literal, not the \0 escape. That made git treat the file as binary, so it would not three-way merge it. The agent found the byte with python, replaced it with the escape and re-merged by hand.
cost_estimate: ~8 tool calls, ~1 min
design_lesson: n/a (tooling): agent file-write tools should escape control characters in source text.

pattern: trusted SHA-based merge check; rebased commits looked unmerged
summary: Asked which local branches could be deleted, the agent relied on `git branch --no-merged` and reported a branch with LED-current work as unmerged. The user doubted this, and a spot check showed all 10 commits had landed on main under different hashes after a rebase, with leds.ts byte-identical.
cost_estimate: 1 extra user round, ~5 min, ~15 tool calls.
design_lesson: Contrast: a query whose name suggests semantic equality ('merged') but which checks identity (SHA reachability) misleads agents; API names should match what they actually test.

pattern: worktree created from stale base despite baseRef:head; repeated rebase/re-create
summary: In at least 9 of the 20 sessions in this batch (D4XC, 014TW, MB7, Eksj, PPUA, QuNL, Adh6, FAaM, U1g; SSM5 also had to rebase before merging because main moved), EnterWorktree created the worktree from a commit 40–54 behind local main. Agents found missing files, then reset, rebased or re-created the worktree, and in U1g resolved multi-file rebase conflicts. The agents diagnosed the cause themselves (cwd in apps/web subdir, so .claude/settings.json baseRef wasn't picked up).
cost_estimate: Typically 5–15 extra tool calls and 1–3 minutes per session. Across the batch that is roughly 80–100 tool calls of pure environment overhead.
design_lesson: Contrast case: tooling whose config resolution depends on cwd fails silently (it 'succeeds' with the wrong base). Agents pay for it on every invocation until the failure is loud.

api: headless Chrome UI tests (CDP, File System Access permission)
pattern: flaky browser UI suite, failing differently each run, including on main
summary: The full UI suite failed three times with three different errors: FSA folder-permission-expired checks, a timeout waiting for zpcrweb.json, and a run timeout. The agent checked machine load, ran the suite on main (which also failed with 'Inspected target navigated or closed'), then landed.
cost_estimate: 4 full UI runs (~80-100 s each), ~12 tool calls
design_lesson: Same family: nondeterministic browser timing in automation multiplies agent verification cost.

api: headless Chrome UI tests (focus, File System Access permission)
pattern: flaky browser UI suite (focus check, FSA 'permission expired' check, well-grid header) needing repeated full reruns
summary: The agent's change passed, but full browser-suite runs failed in different unrelated places each time: well-grid header checks, then the File System Access 'folder permission has expired' checks, then the clone-flow focus check. It took 4 full runs and only passed 'on a quiet machine'. No root cause was found.
cost_estimate: 3 extra full UI runs (~100 s each), ~8 tool calls
design_lesson: Timing-sensitive browser behaviour (focus, permission state, async layout) under load makes agent test loops expensive; observable completion signals beat polling with timeouts.

pattern: no native dual-thumb range input; hand-rolled stacked inputs
summary: The user asked for a double-ended Cq range slider. With no native multi-thumb range control, the agent built one from two stacked <input type=range> elements with transparent, pointer-events:none tracks and grabbable thumbs (~111 lines of CSS and a 118-line component). Driving it from tests needed the HTMLInputElement.prototype value setter plus synthetic input/change events so React would notice. It worked on the first try, so this is a cost rather than a mistake.
cost_estimate: About 230 lines of hand-written UI plumbing and ~11 min for the whole feature, with no rework.
design_lesson: A native multi-value range control would turn a known-fragile CSS hack into one element. Programmatic value changes that fire the same events as user input would remove the prototype-setter trick.

pattern: agent adds a redundant device listing instead of using the live status signal
summary: To make 'Current run: State' show running immediately, the agent made a run start trigger a run-folder listing and landed it. The user rejected that ('The status report tells us the device is not idle, that's enough. Revert this change'). The agent reverted and derived the state from STATUS?'s running flag instead. This repeats the TouLq pattern from about 20 minutes earlier, in a parallel session.
cost_estimate: About 7 minutes over the two attempts (20:05–20:12), roughly 56 tool calls, with two commit/rebase/merge cycles.
design_lesson: Agents reach for extra I/O when unsure which source of truth is authoritative. A protocol doc stating which signal is canonical for each piece of state helps.

pattern: agent invents extra device I/O not in the protocol spec
summary: Asked to drop periodic LISTALLFILES polling in favor of the usb.md signals, the agent replaced it with an extra 'list on run start' edge that usb.md never specified. The user challenged it, the agent admitted it had invented the edge, removed it, and updated the docs.
cost_estimate: The correction turn took about 3 minutes and 23 tool calls, a second commit/merge cycle.
design_lesson: When a spec lists exactly when to perform I/O, agents still add extra calls to be safe. Specs that say clearly which signal is authoritative (STATUS? vs listings) help prevent this.

pattern: guessed legacy library API (usb.findByIds) that no longer exists in current major version
summary: The agent's first Node probe used the legacy node-usb API `usb.findByIds(VID, PID)` and raw endpoint addresses. usb@3 threw `TypeError: usb.findByIds is not a function`. The agent listed the module exports, found the `WebUSB` class, and rewrote the probe against the WebUSB-shaped API, which also became the basis for sharing code with the browser.
cost_estimate: ~4 tool calls, <1 min
design_lesson: A standard API shape (WebUSB) that Node libraries also implement lets an agent reuse one mental model; version-drifted bespoke APIs cause stale-knowledge errors.

pattern: ad-hoc headless-Chrome script misuses project harness; page never loads so a later DOM wait times out
summary: Same failure mode as session_01TVXheWZVVwczwiHrSTL4r7. A one-off screenshot script used dev.url (undefined) instead of dev.base, so the page never loaded and loadFile timed out waiting for input[type=file]. The agent compared against uishot.mjs and fixed it with sed.
cost_estimate: ~2.5 min (19:57:25-19:59:56), 5 tool calls, 2 one-minute timeouts
design_lesson: Silent 'undefined' URLs turn into downstream DOM timeouts; strict, typed navigation APIs would surface the real error immediately.

pattern: ad-hoc headless-Chrome script misuses project harness; page never loads so a later DOM wait times out

It failed 4 times: a relative import path (ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND), then 'timed out waiting for the input[type="file"] file input' twice, then a process-kill error. pattern: guessed helper return shape instead of reading it
summary: In a throwaway CDP script, the agent called the repo's own harness helpers with guessed field names (dev.url instead of dev.base; startChrome without a profile dir). The script failed or timed out, and the agent fixed it after reading the harness source. The same guess recurs across sessions.
cost_estimate: 2-4 tool calls, 1-3 min (the timeouts are 20s+ each)
design_lesson: Contrast case: an untyped JS helper whose returned object's field names must be guessed; typed or self-describing return values would avoid it.

pattern: grep alias silently returns nothing on a large file
summary: grep (aliased to ugrep) returned no matches and no error on the 3,113-line useZpcrStore.ts, so 3 searches came back empty before the agent switched to /usr/bin/grep. The same thing happened in session_0175YV (6bbe4529) and session_01QbeN (446a6c83). Separately, zsh's 'no matches found: --include=*.ts' glob error recurs in many sessions in this batch.
cost_estimate: 3-4 wasted tool calls per occurrence
design_lesson: Silent empty results are worse than errors for an agent; tools should fail loudly.

pattern: library default (auto point markers) not overridden in a new chart builder
summary: The new meltChart.ts omitted `points: { show: false }`, which the existing chart builders set on every series. uPlot then drew a dot at every point of the 61-point melt curves. The user spotted the white dots, and the fix was the one-line option.
cost_estimate: ~4 min, one extra commit and UI run.
design_lesson: Defaults that switch on based on data density surprise both humans and agents. Predictable, explicit defaults are easier to get right.

pattern: unquoted --include=*.tsx fails under zsh nomatch
summary: 'grep -rn ... --include=*.tsx' failed with '(eval):1: no matches found: --include=*.tsx' because zsh expands the unquoted glob. The same error recurs in sessions Ta6VVq7, Q1YjEyoc and 017GP1Sr in this batch, each time costing a retry.
cost_estimate: 1 extra call per occurrence, 3 occurrences in batch.
design_lesson: Not web; contrast example of a recurring environment trap that costs a retry each time.

pattern: unquoted glob in shell flag fails under zsh
summary: In most sessions of this batch (at least 11), the agent ran grep -rn ... --include=*.tsx unquoted. Under the user's zsh this fails with "no matches found" before grep runs. The agent then retried with a different command. The fixes are cheap, but the error recurs constantly.
cost_estimate: ~1 wasted tool call per occurrence, 2-6 per session
design_lesson: Contrast case: environment-dependent syntax (bash vs zsh globbing) produces a misleading error rather than the intended behaviour.

pattern: bash-isms in zsh (== in [ ], unquoted --include=*.ts globs, wrong cwd assumptions)
summary: Across this batch the agent repeatedly ran commands that failed under the user's zsh: `(eval):1: == not found` from `[ x == y ]`, and `no matches found: --include=*.ts` from unquoted globs. There were also many sed/cat 'No such file' errors from a stale cwd after `cd`. Each costs a retry. About 34 zsh errors across 18 of 20 sessions in batch b02 (5 in this session), plus frequent worktree-guard refusals of compound git commands.
cost_estimate: ~1 retry each; ~34 occurrences across the batch, so roughly 34 wasted tool calls.
design_lesson: Environment differences the agent can't see (shell dialect) cost a steady tax. Tools should advertise their dialect up front or fail with a fix-it hint.
